articles.title: France book South Africa rematch in Nations Championship final with bonus-point victory over Argentina
articles.summary: France reached the Nations Championship final after beating Argentina 45-17 with seven tries on Saturday.
articles.body:
France beat Argentina 45-17, securing the bonus-point victory they needed to reach the final of the Nations Championship; France will meet South Africa in the November 29 final at Twickenham; France beat the Springboks 21-19 last week in Paris

France reached the Nations Championship final after beating Argentina 45-17 with seven tries on Saturday.

England's 37-12 win against New Zealand left France needing a bonus-point victory to make the November 29 final against South Africa, who topped the southern hemisphere group despite losing to Ireland.

Already leading 21-10, Emilien Gailleton got France's fourth try for the bonus point in the 64th minute against 14 men, and moments later the yellow card for Pumas prop Mayco Vivas was upgraded to red.

France finished with three more tries. Lock Tyler Duguid charged through following an attacking lineout, centre Kalvin Gourgues showed stunning pace from near halfway to make the left corner, and Louis Bielle-Biarrey completed the rout with his 31st try in 30 tests.

In the first half lock Mickaël Guillard and try-scoring hooker Peato Mauvaka crossed for France. Returning fly-half Matthieu Jalibert cleverly set up silky centre Gourgues shortly after the break for the first of his two tries.

Argentina led briefly at 10-7 for 10 minutes thanks to a converted try from centre Justo Piccardo and a penalty from fly-half Tomas Albornoz.

Jalibert's faster than expected recovery from a torn thigh allowed captain Antoine Dupont to resume at scrum-half after wearing the No 10 jersey a week ago against South Africa.

Dupont showed his class at the end with a kick down the left flank for Bielle-Biarrey's try.

Gourdes nailed five conversions as a makeshift kicker on the night.

Tributes were held before the game for Federico Martín Aramburú, the former Argentina player who died four years ago after being fatally shot in Paris.

articles.title: Nations Championship: Wales fall short in 29-26 defeat to Australia after epic New Zealand victory
articles.summary: Wales failed to back up their epic win over New Zealand as Australia edged their Nations Championship match 29-26 in Cardiff.
articles.body:
Australia narrowly defeated Wales at the Principality stadium in Cardiff; Wales couldn't follow up the previous week's epic victory over New Zealand, their first over the All Blacks since 1953; Wales to face Japan on Finals Weekend with Australia taking on Ireland

Wales failed to back up their epic win over New Zealand as Australia edged their Nations Championship match 29-26 in Cardiff.

A first victory over the All Blacks since 1953 had led to week-long celebrations in Wales.

But Australia, having soaked up fierce first-half pressure, produced some fine attacking rugby after the break to prevent Wales from winning three on the spin for the first time since the 2023 World Cup.

Taniela Tupou, Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Max Jorgensen and Len Ikitau secured a try-bonus point for Australia as Ryan Lonergan and Carter Gordon added nine points with the boot.

Wales also scored four tries through Dewi Lake's double, Blair Murray and Ryan Elias, with Sam Costelow landing three conversions, but fell agonisingly short.

Australia fly-half Carter Gordon scored ⁠a penalty in the 74th minute to give the Wallabies a 29-21 lead, which proved enough for victory despite Wales securing a fourth try ⁠through replacement hooker Elias two minutes ​from time.

Wales battled for the winning score in a dramatic close to the match but their attempt to go the length of the field was ended when the ball was ‌knocked on.

"Wales are a tough outfit. What a match," Ikitau said after he was awarded player of the match.

"It's been a tough couple of weeks for us. I know the heart's always there but when you don't get the results it's pretty disheartening. I'm proud of the boys and proud of the effort today."

articles.title: Ireland 20-17 South Africa: Springboks downed as Andy Farrell's side hold on for big victory in Nations Championship
articles.summary: Robert Baloucoune's brace of tries saw Ireland seal a huge 20-17 victory against South Africa in the Nations Championship.
articles.body:
Ireland hang on to seal three-point victory against South Africa on Saturday in Dublin; Springboks suffer back-to-back losses for first time since 2022 and were without head coach Rassie Erasmus after he was banned for six matches

Robert Baloucoune's brace of tries saw Ireland seal a huge 20-17 victory against South Africa in the Nations Championship.

The bonus point for losing within seven points of Ireland tied the Springboks with New Zealand at the top of the southern hemisphere standings, but a huge points differential separated them.

The world champion Springboks will face England or France in the final next Saturday at Twickenham but will go in with consecutive defeats for the first time in four years.

After losing to Six Nations champion France 21-19 last weekend, South Africa was expected to overpower Ireland as they did with embarrassing ease a year ago in Dublin.

But while the forwards set up both tries for South Africa, the backline attack was poor, as it was in Paris. The Springboks lost the aerial battle, struggled with Ireland's defensive line speed, and were flattered in the end to lose by only three points. The Boks led for only four minutes in the game.

They surged late into the match, with Malcolm Marx crossing on 58 minutes to set up a tense finish.

Despite a barrage of South Africa attacks, Ireland's defence was resolute, with Farrell's side moving above France to second in the northern hemisphere standings, with Les Bleus playing Argentina later on Saturday.

Farrell dubbed the victory "remarkable" and hailed his team for their performance against the world champions.

"These boys have done a lot of exceptional things over the years, but certainly in the last 12 months [this is the best]," the Ireland head coach said.

"You always want to test yourself against the best. They are world champions, and not only that, they are the world No 1, and rightly so.

"This was always a challenge we were going to look forward to, and see if we could front up. These games matter.

"The game wasn't perfect, but it was never going to be. Most of the games at the top level aren't."

O'Driscoll: 'Outstanding' Ireland the better attacking team

Former Ireland captain Brian O'Driscoll said to ITV:

"We've been treated to a number of these big days in the last 10 years in Dublin, but this one is right up there.

"I said before the game, South Africa are completely the best team in the world, with the consistency they've shown.

"Ireland today were outstanding. You have to credit Ireland rather than saying where it went wrong for South Africa.

"Ireland looked the better attacking team, and they won the battle in the air.

"We've all been querying, where are we [Ireland]? This was the litmus test and you really discover where you're at.

"With all the hype this week, they did their talking on the pitch.

"The scoreline might even have flattered South Africa. Ireland showed most of the attacking threat."

articles.title: Ryan Crowley: Airman's rugby career has taken off at Leicester Tigers
articles.summary: BBC Sport meets Ryan Crowley, the airman whose rugby career has taken off at Prem giants Leicester Tigers.
articles.body:
Corporal Ryan Crowley has spent a decade helping get aircraft off the ground.

It has taken just as long for the winger to finally get his professional rugby union career to take off.

It was only a year ago that Crowley was plucked from his role as an avionics engineer with the Royal Air Force and recruited by Leicester Tigers.

The 28-year-old Welshman was handed a deal with the giants of the game, the 11-time Prem champions - when he didn't even know one was up for grabs.

"I thought I got sent up to Tigers to go and get experience and do a pre-season with a pro team," he told BBC Sport.

The military man had simply followed orders.

Chinnor, the second division side he was playing for, asked him to join Geoff Parling's Tigers for the early weeks of their Prem Rugby Cup campaign last season.

"After a couple of weeks Geoff said, 'you've been successful in your trial', and I was like, 'what trial?'," Crowley added.

"The silver lining to not knowing it was a trial is I had no pressure on me; I just came up and I was just trying to learn as much as I could.

"I didn't have any expectations of having to come out the end of it with something, but luckily I did."

Winger Crowley joins Tigers after successful trial

Listen to the Tigers Rugby Show on BBC Radio Leicester

Crowley saw out the season with Tigers, playing seven Prem Rugby Cup games, and was handed a new one-year deal to remain with the club this term.

It was after that contract extension that Crowley was able to tell Parling what it meant to him to be a full-time professional after years of dedication to the British Armed Forces.

Even now Crowley remains part of the RAF.

But through its elite athlete scheme, he has been allowed to step back from his role to pursue his playing career with Tigers.

"When Geoff told me he wanted me to stay, I said to him that for a very young Ryan Crowley this was a dream come true," the winger explained.

"I did think my ship had sailed - but I kept training and kept going."

Crowley grew up playing for St Peter's in Cardiff and had a spell with Welsh Premiership side Pontypridd before enlisting to become an airman when he was still a teenager.

At that point, rugby became something he did alongside his basic training at RAF Halton in Buckinghamshire and his studies in avionics, which took him to RAF Cosford in Shropshire.

For much of the next 10 years his focus was on carrying out maintenance and repairs on the sophisticated electronics on military aircraft - which has included Boeing C-17 Globemaster military transporters worth more than £250m.

And yet, his career in the military was never an excuse to give up on making it as a rugby player.

The RAF has played a significant role in that, with Crowley representing them in inter-services matches, while he has also played on the global stage for the UK Armed Forces.

During the three years he spent becoming a fully qualified aircraft engineer he was playing club rugby in the lower leagues, but after that he leaped up the divisions when signed by second-tier side London Scottish in 2020.

It had appeared to be a career breakthrough.

But funding cuts by English rugby's governing body, the Rugby Football Union (RFU), that same year, as well as the financial fallout of the Covid-19 pandemic, forced the club to shift from being a full-time professional outfit to a part-time, semi-professional side by the time Crowley joined them.

"I'd often say to my family that I felt like I had the worst luck in rugby," Crowley said.

"I was always close to something happening, like with what happened at London Scottish, then I'd miss out. I've had injuries at different times that have also stopped me from taking opportunities.

"But I've not given up and have always kept knocking on the door. I didn't really see any other choice - rugby is my life and I kept playing. I've been obsessed with rugby since I was old enough to pick a ball up and throw it around.

"And it's finally worked out for me and I've got to where I want to be."

'I'm competing against myself, learning from them'

At Tigers he has taken his place among a stable of international wingers, including Wales' Gabriel Hamer-Webb and England pair Adam Radwan and Ollie Hassell-Collins.

Crowley has so far featured 10 times for Tigers, with all those appearances coming in the Prem Cup.

And while he was named in a matchday squad for a European Champions Cup match last season, he never made it off the bench.

"It's been challenging, but I wouldn't say challenging in a negative way," Crowley said.

"Having the likes of Radas, Hass and Gabe in front of me, I never really came into this thinking I'm competing against them. And while I actually am, I'm competing against myself to see how far I can get.

"I'm learning from them because they've been in the system and this environment for so long.

"There is a lot of healthy competition in the team but we are all extremely close - with lots of group chats and good banter as we wind each other up.

"When we step on to that pitch we do drive each other, the switch gets flicked and we are on it, but as soon as we are off it we are back to the jokes."

And how does being a corporal in the RAF, who has turned into a Tigers winger, fare when it comes to the mickey-taking of team-mates?

It turns out that while he has managed to fly under the radar by avoiding any military-style nicknames, his team-mates have instead chosen to lean into his 5ft 7in (1.7m) stature instead.

"I do get the banter about my height, but I'm an easy target for that one," he said.

"I just kind of live it and wear it as a badge to be fair because being probably one of the smallest people in the Prem, to be at this level, I think, is an achievement."

articles.title: Rassie Erasmus: South Africa coach invites fans to watch-along of Springboks clash vs Ireland following six-match ban
articles.summary: Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus was handed a six-match suspension for comments he made about referees following South Africa's Nations Championship defeat by France; South Africa Rugby have requested a full hearing into his ban
articles.body:
Erasmus had questioned whether there were double standards in the officiating of South Africa's 21-19 defeat to France during a press conference earlier in the week, prompting an investigation from World Rugby , who later said that the coach had "disrespected the authority of the officials".

He will now be unable to have any match-day involvement in his side's Nations Championship match against Ireland on Saturday, or their Nations Championship Finals match, commencing the following week.

South Africa have requested a full hearing in response to the sanction and on Wednesday, Erasmus broke his silence, inviting members of the public to join him to watch Saturday's game via a live stream.

"Can sit and moan or make the best of it," the Springboks coach wrote in a post on X.

"I'll be watching the match at the hotel. Not keen to watch [it] on my own.

"So, let's give it a go and hope I get the 'tech' sorted = TV on, My Laptop camera on, and you're welcome to join me.

"Sign up here (adults 18+): . This is personal, not official."

On his streaming website, Erasmus has embedded a video of a flying South Africa flag, with a link to sign up to watch.

The 54-year-old, who guided South Africa to back-to-back Rugby World Cups in 2019 and 2023, provided some more details on the webpage about how the live stream would work.

"We each watch on our own TV, and I'll be on camera so you can see me watch it too. Send me a message and I'll read some out."

A disclaimer on the page read: "This is me personally, Rassie. It is not an official team or Springbok channel."

It is unclear when Erasmus will be able to return to coach South Africa, but he is expected to be available for the 2027 Rugby World Cup.

On Tuesday, World Rugby confirmed an independent panel had reviewed the comments made by Erasmus under World Rugby's Match Official Abuse Sanction Process, a framework that was introduced in July.

"The panel determined that the comments suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match, and when the conduct is considered as a whole a reasonable person would conclude that the conduct constituted an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the match officials," the governing body said in a statement.

"In respect to the sanction, the panel determined that the conduct clearly amounts to disrespecting the authority of the match officials by impugning their integrity."

Erasmus: Manipulation of the game or the result?

On Monday, Erasmus claimed France should have been given three yellow cards for illegal tackles as he leapt into a rant criticising referees.

"Let's say 11 of those were at least a penalty and three I thought were at least three yellow cards. And not one was sanctioned and not one was shown out or cited," Erasmus said.

"I'll send you the playlist, but I'll get into trouble… So I can't send the playlist to anybody and we can only send five clips to World Rugby. So we'll probably query it, but the answer will probably be: 'Yes, it was a mistake; it should have been penalised'.

"On numerous times we mentioned to the referee 'we think there's a knee-drop tackle'. I'm saying to you, my feeling is that knee-drop tackles is out. They happened 17 times in our game. Not one was penalised.

"And if the TMO didn't see it, then maybe technology must be better. If he saw it and ignored it, what does that boil down to? Manipulation of the game or the result? Or players getting injured?

"So, all I'm asking is don't take the TMOs out and discourage them from getting involved. Then the wrong team will win and players will get injured. That's all I'm saying."

World Rugby has since received backlash on social media in the wake of Erasmus' ban, and South Africa Rugby has condemned the abuse.

"SA Rugby unequivocally condemns any form of intimidation, threats or personal attacks. Such behaviour has no place in rugby and is entirely contrary to the values upon which our game is founded."

articles.title: England v New Zealand: Jack van Poortvliet on 2022 All Blacks nightmare
articles.summary: Jack van Poortvliet was picked off and subbed off when he last met the All Blacks. Four years on, he says the experience made him a better player.
articles.body:
A mocking pat on the back from Codie Taylor. A close-up of his own face on the Twickenham big screen. A painful inquest under the sticks.

Jack van Poortvliet's first meeting with New Zealand was only four minutes old when it curdled sour.

In November 2022 Van Poortvliet, then 21, was winning only his sixth cap.

Sharing the scrum-half duties with England veterans Ben Youngs and Richard Wigglesworth, he had been a key part in Leicester's run to the Premiership title the previous season. Van Poortvliet was touted as the next big thing at Test level too.

But, off an early England line-out, Van Poortvliet, focused on Owen Farrell's hands, failed to spot Dalton Papali'i flying up out of the line.

The All Black flanker picked off the interception and cantered in for the game's opening try.

Van Poortvliet's afternoon ended after 54 minutes. With England trailing 22-6, his final act was a knock-on after being harried by Brodie Retallick at the back of a breakdown. His mistake squandered a prime attacking position.

Eddie Jones had seen enough, withdrawing Van Poortvliet and bringing on Ben Youngs.

England would go on to draw the game 25-25 after a remarkable late rally. But there was no rallying Van Poortvliet.

"I remember just being pretty disappointed," he told BBC Sport.

"It was the first time I had felt what it was like to play for my country and not deliver how I wanted to.

"I care a lot about how I play and how I perform. At that time, I wasn't very good at letting stuff go or managing how I was when things went against me. I remember being pretty down."

It was a difficult time for England as a whole.

Van Poortvliet retained his place, but a 27-13 defeat by South Africa the following weekend signalled the end of Jones' England reign. An eyesore of a Six Nations campaign, including a record 53-10 home defeat by France, followed a few months later.

Van Poortvliet, who had read online praise on his rise to Test level, was now exposed to keyboard criticism.

When he suffered a serious ankle injury in a warm-up Test against Wales before the 2023 World Cup, he received posts celebrating his absence from the tournament.

But Van Poortvliet says his performance against New Zealand, and the criticism that followed, was the start of learning to leave mistakes in the past.

"It was probably a good thing that I had that [performance against New Zealand] so early on," he said.

"I probably stopped taking myself so seriously and gained the ability to let go [of past mistakes] in game.

"You're not defined by one moment in a game. If there's a couple of errors, mistakes happen. You're never going to play the perfect game. It was one of those big lessons for me."

Alex Mitchell leapt to the top of England's scrum-half pecking order at France 2023.

But Mitchell's injuries, combined with Van Poortvliet's smart form for table-topping Leicester, mean the Tigers man is back in possession of England's number nine shirt.

Van Poortvliet made only his third England start since 2023 in July's Nations Championship opener against South Africa and has been in place ever since.

Presuming he retains his spot, Saturday will be his first encounter with New Zealand since his 2022 horror show.

Listen to match commentary on BBC Radio 5 Extra, BBC Sounds, BBC Sport website and through your smart speaker

The All Blacks are recovering from their own, more recent, disappointment.

Coach Dave Rennie said his players "let their country down" in a shock defeat by Wales last weekend.

Van Poortvliet expects them to react with the level-headedness he himself has learned.

"They had a disappointing result last week, which happens. We've had plenty in the past," he said.

"Most good teams don't have two poor performances in a row and good teams normally respond well.

"We're excited to take on the best version of New Zealand."

After Cortez Ratima deputised in defeat by Wales, Van Poortvliet is likely to be up against Cam Roigard, whose relatively tall stature and running game are a similar match to his own.

But, four years on and with the World Cup looming once more, England are also seeing the best version of Van Poortvliet again.

articles.title: PWR: RFU wants to 'protect Red Roses' with reduction in international players
articles.summary: The RFU wants PWR to protect the interests of England's Red Roses, which could see a reduction in the number of international players in the league.
articles.body:
World rugby has endured a few shocks and upsets in 2026 - and England's women losing back-to-back Test matches to Canada was among the biggest.

But with 25 Canadians plying their trade on English soil in Premiership Women's Rugby (PWR) last season, their success on the international stage comes at a time when PWR has been in discussions with the Rugby Football Union (RFU) to review the numbers of overseas players in the league.

"We are keen to attract star talent into PWR to continue to make it the best league in the world," said RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney.

"But we've also got to protect England Red Roses' interests as well."

Changes have been planned for the 2027-28 PWR season around injury dispensation for foreign players, with the removal of club injury credit which helps to cover the cost of replacing an injured player.

Only players who sustain an injury while on international duty for one of England's representative teams will be eligible.

However, discussions have gone further around the numbers of English Qualified Players (EQP) required in matchday squads.

Speaking to BBC Sport, Sweeney said: "We're talking about it. Currently, there's 13 EQP in PWR. It's 15 in the [men's] Prem.

"We're always concerned about the amount of game time that's occurring for under-23 players coming through the system. Are they getting enough game time?

"We're having conversations with PWR in terms of how we can maximise that, so it is a live topic."

No panic for England but Mitchell issues PWR warning

Bristol will 'bring out' best version of Kildunne

England had been on a 41-match unbeaten streak - dating back almost four years - before twice losing to Canada in the WXV Global Series last month.

It prompted a warning from head coach John Mitchell that too many overseas players in the PWR could be detrimental for future Red Roses sides.

The league has increasingly attracted the best global talent. In recent years, a majority of Scotland and Wales players have played in PWR and since the 2025 World Cup, more players have joined from New Zealand.

The highest-profile arrival last season was Black Ferns captain Ruahei Demant linking up with Bristol, while Ruby Tui has joined Trailfinders Women for the new campaign.

And while many neutrals believe Canada's growing success is good for the women's game, Sweeney says England must keep "raising the bar".

"It doesn't feel it's good for the game for us, we never want to lose - but it had to come at some stage," he said.

"Seeing the growth in the Canadian team, largely due to where they play in PWR - it's encouraging that the standards are rising.

"We're conscious that unions like Ireland are investing much more heavily now into the women's game as well, so it is good for the game.

"From our perspective, we just want to keep raising the bar and challenging people to catch us and challenge us."

IRFU await news of 'massive opportunity' to join PWR

Fewer international stars would 'diminish quality of PWR'

Canada and Saracens scrum-half Olivia Apps was named PWR player of the season when her club lifted the 2025-26 trophy.

She says exposure to the PWR has massively benefited Canadian rugby.

"It's the best women's league right now to play in and the best quality competition," she told BBC Sport.

"We don't have a league back home, so to be able to come from the universities and play with and against the best players in the world is going to make us better for sure."

Asked if she was worried Canadian players would not get as much game time in the future, Apps said: "I would hope not. I think that would diminish the quality of the PWR.

"Internationals make this league what it is, and credit to the English players, but the internationals really do contribute in a great way.

"Any coach or team that has a Canadian on their side loves to have that Canadian because they work hard, they bring the physicality, the athleticism and a great style of rugby."

Reducing foreign imports would allow young English talent more PWR game time, but the move does not come without concerns.

"The league itself is to create Red Roses and to create English players for the future. If we are going to bring non-EQP players into the league, then they have to add to the league, so they have to be of a world-class standard," said Loughborough Lightning head coach Nathan Smith.

But Smith does envisage a problem if the league changes before investing in the pathways.

"There's a pinch point at the start of next season where we'll have Lions, England camp and a Premiership Cup. My simple question is, are there enough players to fulfil all three?" he said.

"England Under-20s and Under-18s aren't performing on the world stage, therefore what can we do to support that? We need a level of competition that sits below the PWR that fulfils their needs for development."

A PWR spokesperson said: "There is no difference of opinion between us and the RFU on this and developing the next generation of Red Roses is a specific, stated objective of the PWR.

"We will continue to work collaboratively with the RFU on EQP and any other matter which is important to the future of women's rugby in this country."

The new PWR season starts on Friday as Loughborough Lightning host Trailfinders.

For now, overseas stars will remain a key part of the league's success, but how many are allowed to feature in the future may define its next chapter.

articles.title: Ireland v South Africa: Rassie Erasmus ban 'not dominating the coffee room' - Timoney
articles.summary: Ireland back row Nick Timoney says players are "not living under a rock" but any talk of Rassie Erasmus' six-game ban is not dominating their conversations.
articles.body:
Ireland back row Nick Timoney says players are "not living under a rock" but any talk of Rassie Erasmus' six-game ban is not dominating their conversations.

South Africa will face Ireland on Saturday in Dublin without their head coach after Erasmus was sanctioned for a third time by World Rugby.

Speaking at a news conference in Dublin on Monday, Erasmus questioned what he perceived as double standards in officiating to the point where he asked: "Is that not match-fixing?"

"You'd be amazed at how little rugby players are in the online rugby space," Timoney said when asked about the 54-year-old's comments.

"You tend to, for whatever reason, avoid it as best you can. Just more so you don't see the player ratings after a bad loss, or whatever it is.

"Obviously, I'm sure we're not living under a rock here but it's certainly not dominating the coffee room, you could say."

Before his match-fixing comments, Erasmus predicted that Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast would not be banned for a hip-drop tackle against Fiji because of a "technicality".

On Wednesday, World Rugby confirmed the 23-year-old would be free to face the back-to-back world champions on Saturday [16:40 GMT].

"It's kind of what we expected but I'm delighted for Sam and the rest of us," added Timoney.

"It's good it's over with nice and early in the week so we can focus on the game."

Divide and conquer - now maverick Erasmus plans online watchalong

'Is that not match-fixing?' - Erasmus questions officiating

Andy Farrell will name his side to face the Springboks on Thursday at 14:00 GMT.

Timoney said it was "an enormous game" as Ireland look to finish the Nations Championship with a third win in a row.

After wins over Australia and Japan were followed by a loss to New Zealand, Farrell's side have started November's window with victories over Argentina and Fiji.

Both Ireland and South Africa, who lost to France in their last match, have the opportunity to finish top of their respective northern and southern hemisphere groups.

When asked if Ireland were still hurting from their defeat by the Springboks in Dublin last year - when the visitors ran out 24-13 winners - Timoney looked at the bigger picture.

"I think we're hurting from not quite being where we want to be," he added.

"We obviously want to be the best team in the world like everyone else does. Being 100% honest, we're probably not quite there yet even though we have been in the past.

"There's no shying away from the fact they beat us at home last year. There's all sorts of points we want to prove but largely to ourselves."

Timoney, who has started Ireland's last 10 Tests, said the versatility of Saturday's opponents is one of their major strengths.

"They've not become double world champions by having one easy trick to beating them.

"We've just got to be excellent in all areas and it's going to take a massive effort certainly."

He added that Ireland are "pretty confident with our plan going in" and they have been building towards the final match in Dublin, before the Nations Championships' finals weekend in London.

"We're really looking forward to it and we've been building towards it. The last 12-24 months haven't been 100% what we've wanted the whole time.

"We feel like we're building nicely. The coaching, the players within the group, they're all world class. We can only be going in the right direction."

articles.title: Wales v Australia: Steve Tandy makes four changes to side that beat All Blacks
articles.summary: Wales make four changes to their starting line-up that beat the All Blacks for the Nations Championship meeting with Australia.
articles.body:
Wales have made four changes to the side that made history against New Zealand for the Nations Championship fixture against Australia.

Head coach Steve Tandy has tinkered with the starting line-up that beat the All Blacks for the first time in 73 years at Principality Stadium.

Wales go with the same XV that opened the Nations Championship with a 28-21 victory against Japan.

Alex Mann comes in for James Botham at blind-side flanker, Aaron Wainwright is back from a leg injury at number eight, lock Ben Carter returns for the injured Adam Beard and Josh Adams gets the nod on the wing.

Botham was man of the match against New Zealand but his partner is expecting their first child this week.

Listen live on BBC Radio Wales, BBC Radio Cymru and Sports Extra on BBC Sounds

Exeter flanker Kane James is set to win his second cap from the bench after making his debut against Argentina in July.

Scarlets centre or fly-half Joe Hawkins also comes in for Ospreys playmaker Dan Edwards, who suffered an ankle injury in training that has led to Cardiff's Jarrod Evans being called into the Nations Championship squad.

Taine Plumtree will cover the second row in the absence of Beard, who suffered a shoulder injury against New Zealand.

Number eight Taine Basham and wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb drop out of the matchday squad after starting against the All Blacks.

Eleven players will have started all three Tests - eight from English clubs and the Scarlets trio of full-back Blair Murray, centre Eddie James and fly-half Sam Costelow.

Rees-Zammit: From beating All Blacks to meeting Man Utd heroes

Wales show they have bench impact in All Blacks win

After beating Japan and the All Blacks, Wales are looking to complete a Cardiff hat-trick against the Wallabies.

They then travel to Twickenham's Allianz Stadium for finals weekend when they will play a southern hemisphere opponent, which could well be another fixture against the Japanese.

Head coach Tandy said: "We were all immensely proud to make history last week.

"There's a new opportunity and challenge for us against Australia and we're looking to back up our performance this weekend.

"It's our last home game of this competition. The support that fans give to the players and staff has been incredible and we can't wait to get back out at Principality Stadium."

The Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) has stated it has already sold more than 60,000 tickets for the fixture at Principality Stadium, which holds just under 74,000.

That figure exceeds the 55,152 that witnessed history against the All Blacks, despite the late kick-off time against the Wallabies.

Exeter's Tom Hooper has been named in the second row for Australia while flanker Carlo Tizzano starts in five forward changes from the team that lost to Scotland.

The front rows rotate roles for this Test with Isaac Kailea, Brandon Paenga-Amosa and Taniela Tupou selected as the starting combination, with Angus Bell, Billy Pollard and Allan Alaalatoa the replacements.

Lock Jeremy Williams and Fraser McReight are also on the bench as Australia contend with a six-day turnaround.

Wallabies head coach Les Kiss said: "We know we need to step up against a Welsh team full of confidence and momentum after their historic win against the All Blacks last weekend.

"Pulling on the gold jersey against Wales at Principality Stadium in Cardiff creates one of the great atmospheres in world rugby and we are focused on being up for the occasion."

articles.summary: Ireland hooker and captain Dan Sheehan has been shifted out of position to start at No 8 for the visit of South Africa to Dublin in Saturday's Nations Championship (4.40pm) in unusual and risky Andy Farrell move; Fly-half Sam Prendergast starts after citing against him dismissed
articles.body:
The unusual move, with Sheehan's ordinary position at hooker, comes with Ireland missing trio Caelan Doris, Jack Conan and Sean Jansen due to injury.

Sheehan has only played at No 8 once in his career to date, starting there for Leinster against Munster in last month's URC contest at the Aviva Stadium - a clash in which Leinster badly lost the breakdown battle before coming through to win.

Other changes see full-back Hugo Keenan, centre Robbie Henshaw and lock Joe McCarthy return to the squad to start.

Fly-half Sam Prendergast starts the contest after a citing against him for a hip-drop tackle was dismissed on Wednesday .

Wings Rob Baloucoune and Mack Hansen remain to form the back-three with Keenan, while Stuart McCloskey - who played most of last week's victory over Fiji off the bench - partners Henshaw in midfield.

Scrum-half Jamison Gibson-Park retains his starting place, with Craig Casey staying on the bench.

Into the forwards, Ronan Kelleher starts at hooker with Sheehan at No 8, while props Andrew Porter and Tadhg Furlong start either side of Kelleher in the front-row.

Tadhg Beirne starts again in the second row, alongside McCarthy, while Ryan Baird starts at blindside flanker and Josh van der Flier at openside ahead of Nick Timoney.

On the bench, replacement tighthead Sam Illo has been passed fit to be involved, while hooker Tom Stewart, loosehead Tom O'Toole, lock James Ryan, fly-half Ciaran Frawley and centre Bundee Aki complete the squad alongside Timoney and Casey.

Springboks recall Etzebeth for crunch clash with Ireland in Dublin

For South Africa, they have recalled experienced lock Eben Etzebeth for the Nations ‌Championship Test in Dublin, one of five changes to the starting XV ‌that lost to France in Paris.

Etzebeth is set to extend his ​Springbok record to 148 caps by partnering Ruan Nortje in the second row, with Cameron Hanekom coming ​in at No 8 as Jasper Wiese serves a four-match suspension after his red card against the French.

Props Ox Nche and ​Wilco Louw plus hooker Malcolm Marx, who were originally selected as the front row last weekend before being replaced just before ​kick-off in a tactical switch, have been named ⁠in the starting XV again.

The ⁠backline remains the same with Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu at fly-half and Morne van den Berg the preferred ‌scrum-half.

South Africa will likely need to beat Ireland to reach the Nations Championship final, although a losing bonus point could be ‌enough if England defeat New Zealand and deny the All Blacks any bonus points.

"This is a massive match for us and we know the magnitude of facing Ireland in Dublin, so we felt ⁠it was important to strike a balance between consistency ​in selection, while managing some players and giving ​others who have been training hard and putting up ​their hands a chance in what will be a challenging ⁠encounter," coach Rassie Erasmus said.

articles.title: Ireland v South Africa: Hosts name Dan Sheehan at number eight for Nations Championship match
articles.summary: Ireland captain Dan Sheehan is named at number eight for Saturday's highly anticipated Nations Championship match against world champions South Africa in Dublin.
articles.body:
Ireland captain Dan Sheehan has been named at number eight for Saturday's highly anticipated Nations Championship match against world champions South Africa in Dublin.

Having won all 42 of his previous caps at hooker, the 28-year-old returns after recovering from a concussion to partner flankers Ryan Baird and Josh van der Flier in the back row.

Ireland head coach Andy Farrell has faced an injury crisis at number eight with regular skipper Caelan Doris, Jack Conan, Sean Jansen and recent debutant James McNabney all ruled out.

Nick Timoney, who was handed the jersey for last week's victory over Fiji, drops to the bench.

With Doris and Conan unavailable, Sheehan anchored the scrum in Leinster's United Rugby Championship win over Munster last month, but Saturday will be his first Test run-out in the back row.

"Most people would agree that he [Sheehan]'s a world-class player, not just good," said Farrell, who did not wish to comment on South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus' six-match ban for questioning the integrity of match officials.

"Throwing the ball in or scrummaging, his point of difference is in and around the field and how he plays the game with ball in hand or defensively, running lines and all of that.

"That's suited to number eight. He was training there all last week because he was on the 12-day return-to-play protocols, so we had a bit of a head start there, and he played there recently.

"He's very cool, calm and collected; there's no arrogance there whatsoever. Things don't bother him, so he takes it all in his stride, fully confident in his own ability."

South Africa head coach Erasmus banned for six matches

Ireland fly-half Prendergast cleared to face South Africa

SA recall Etzebeth as Erasmus defends late changes

Sheehan's move means that Ronan Kelleher keeps his place at hooker after starting the Fiji game, again joining props Andrew Porter and Tadhg Furlong in the front row.

After being rested last week, Joe McCarthy returns to the second row to partner Tadhg Beirne, with Van der Flier edging out Timoney for the number seven jersey.

Sam Prendergast starts at fly-half after being cleared to face the Springboks on Wednesday, with Jamison Gibson-Park retained at scrum-half.

Prendergast, 23, was cited for his hip-drop tackle on Fiji's Peceli Yato - which was not punished on the pitch - but an independent disciplinary panel ruled the challenge was not worthy of a red card.

"Nothing's changed for us all week," Farrell said when asked about the possibility of a Prendergast ban.

"There's always something going on, whether it's dealing with HIA (head injury assessment) injuries or incidents like we've had with Sam this week.

"It (the hearing) was late on Tuesday night; we trained Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday and Sam's done all of that so there's been no hiccups for us, let's say that."

Robbie Henshaw and Stuart McCloskey both return to midfield after Farrell opted to pair Jamie Osborne and Bundee Aki in a new-look centre partnership against Fiji.

However, Osborne was replaced by McCloskey in the third minute after sustaining a pectoral injury that has ruled him out of the South Africa game, while Aki drops to the bench.

With Hugo Keenan returning to full-back for his 50th cap after sitting out the Fiji game, Mack Hansen switches to the left wing with Robert Baloucoune retained on the right. Tommy O'Brien, who scored two tries from the left wing against Fiji, drops out of the squad.

Farrell has opted for a split of five forwards and three backs on the bench. Tom Stewart, Tom O'Toole, Sam Illo, James Ryan and Timoney provide pack cover with Craig Casey, Ciaran Frawley and Aki named as backline reinforcements.

South Africa, who named their team on Monday, make five changes with record cap holder Eben Etzebeth recalled to the second row.

Cameron Hanekom is named at number eight, replacing Jasper Wiese, who was handed a four-week suspension after being sent off for a dangerous clear-out in last week's defeat by France.

Ox Nche, Malcolm Marx and Wilco Louw are named as the starting front row.

Erasmus also named Nche, Marx and Louw to start the France game but swapped them out for Jan-Hendrik Wessels, Gerhard Steenekamp and Thomas du Toit shortly before kick-off at the Stade de France.

As part of the six-game ban handed down by World Rugby on Tuesday, Erasmus is not permitted to attend the Aviva Stadium encounter.

The 54-year-old has since announced he will be hosting an online watchalong of the match while he watches from his team's Dublin hotel.

South Africa sit second in the Nations Championship southern hemisphere standings, a point adrift of New Zealand.

A South Africa win over Ireland coupled with England beating the All Blacks (Saturday, 14:10 GMT) would be enough for Erasmus' side to seal a place in the 29 November final against the top-ranked northern hemisphere side at Twickenham.

Ireland must beat the Springboks and hope France and England falter against Argentina and New Zealand to finish top.

The Springboks won 24-13 at Aviva Stadium last year, their first victory over Ireland in Dublin since 2012.

articles.body:
Joseph, who missed out on a place in England's matchday 23 for their 45-22 defeat of Australia a fortnight ago , started in last week's crushing 78-15 success over Japan, scoring five tries.

The 24-year-old picked up just his second Test cap in that victory at Twickenham, and his first since July 2022 under Eddie Jones. He moves from right to left wing for the visit of the All Blacks.

Elsewhere fly-half Smith, full-back George Furbank, wing Tommy Freeman, centre Seb Atkinson, hooker Jamie George, props Fin Baxter and Joe Heyes and back-rowers Ollie Chessum and Ben Curry all return as part of nine changes by Steve Borthwick.

Pollock, who made just his second Test start for England in 15 caps last week, drops down to the replacements bench.

Outside-centre Henry Slade, scrum-half Jack van Poortvliet, lock and captain Maro Itoje, second-row Alex Coles - who shifts back alongside Itoje from blindside flanker - and No 8 Ben Earl keep their places.

Alongside Pollock, the replacements bench is made up of hooker Luke Cowan-Dickie, loosehead Ellis Genge, tighthead Will Stuart, lock George Martin, back-row Greg Fisilau, scrum-half Ben Spencer and fly-half/full-back Marcus Smith.

"There are few bigger occasions in international rugby than facing New Zealand," said Borthwick.

"It's a fixture that always carries a special significance, and one that the players are hugely looking forward to.

"We know the quality New Zealand have in their team. We've prepared for the very best version of them, knowing the challenge they will bring and the level we'll need to reach to get the result we want."

articles.title: England vs New Zealand: George Furbank and Ollie Chessum back
articles.summary: England are boosted by the recovery and return of George Furbank, Seb Atkinson and Ollie Chessum to face New Zealand
articles.body:
England have been boosted by the recovery and return of George Furbank, Seb Atkinson and Ollie Chessum to their starting line-up to face New Zealand on Saturday in the Nations Championship.

The trio, who all missed last weekend's win over Japan with knocks, are joined in the starting line-up by Will Joseph, who crossed for five tries against the Brave Blossoms.

Furbank held off the challenge of Freddie Steward, who impressed against Japan, to regain the full-back slot, while vice-captain Chessum brings ballast to a back row that is completed by Ben Curry and Ben Earl.

Fin Smith returns at fly-half to reprise a 10-12 combination with Atkinson that has started six of England's last seven Tests and dates back to their days as teenagers in Worcester Warriors academy.

Barring Joseph's inclusion for the injured Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, England have named the same matchday 23 which combined excellently in the 45-12 victory over Australia a fortnight ago.

After last year's 33-19 success, England are aiming for successive wins over the All Blacks for the first time since beating them in November 2002 and June 2003 - five months before Rugby World Cup glory in Australia.

"There are few bigger occasions in international rugby than facing New Zealand," said head coach Steve Borthwick.

"It's a fixture that always carries a special significance, and one that the players are hugely looking forward to.

"We know the quality New Zealand have in their team. We've prepared for the very best version of them, knowing the challenge they will bring and the level we'll need to reach to get the result we want."

New Zealand, meanwhile, have also been bolstered by the return of big names.

Listen to match commentary on BBC Radio 5 Extra, BBC Sounds, BBC Sport website and through your smart speaker

Following their shock defeat by Wales in Cardiff last weekend, Jordie Barrett, Damian McKenzie and Cam Roigard are brought back in, while wing Will Jordan - his country's leading all-time try-scorer - has recovered from a hamstring issue to start.

Full-back Beauden Barrett, who skippered the side for the first time in Cardiff, will win his 150th Test cap, becoming only the fourth men's player - alongside Alun Wyn Jones, James Slipper and Sam Whitelock - to achieve the landmark.

Beauden and Jordie Barrett's brother Scott is in the second row, while Codie Taylor captains from hooker.

New Zealand lead the Nations Championship southern hemisphere standings by one point and any sort of victory over England is likely to be enough to book their place in the headline fixture of next weekend's play-off finals.

France, who lead the northern hemisphere table and play Argentina later on Saturday, would be their likeliest opponents.

A victory for England, however, could mean Borthwick's men forcing their way into the title play-off, while Ireland and South Africa, who meet in Dublin at 16:40 GMT, could also have a say in an intriguing finale to the group stage.

articles.title: Rassie Erasmus: Eddie Jones says South Africa coach 'overstepped the mark' with criticism of match officials
articles.summary: Rassie Erasmus was handed a six-game ban for his extraordinary criticisms about officials; the South Africa coach claimed there were 17 illegal tackles during his side's defeat to France; Jones says he might tune in to watch Erasmus' live watch along of Ireland vs South Africa
articles.body:
Erasmus hit out at the officiating during his side's 21-19 defeat to France in a press conference on Monday , suggesting officials missed 17 illegal hip-drop tackles before questioning whether "manipulation of the game" was behind why these incidents were not penalised.

Writing in his column for The Daily Mail , Jones expressed sympathy for the Springboks coach, who is barred from attending his side's Nations Championship game against Ireland in Dublin on Saturday, but said his "match-fixing" claims were "inappropriate".

"As coaches, we're only human. We can all get emotional and tip over the edge," Jones wrote.

"There's a lot of pressure in Test rugby, especially if you're coaching one of the big nations.

"But Rassie has definitely overstepped the mark this time. To use cricket parlance, he's bowled a few no-balls in his career. And this is the latest."

While he won't be at the Arriva Stadium come Saturday, Jones believes Erasmus will still have a large influence on South Africa's preparations.

On Wednesday, Erasmus took to X to reveal he'd be hosting a watch along of the match , and invited social media users to join and listen to him watch the game from his hotel room.

Jones believes Erasmus will "still be busy" despite the ban, and added he may even tune in for some of the South Africa coaches' watch along on Saturday after Japan's game against Scotland.

"I wouldn't put it past him for the Springboks to smuggle him into the ground, a la Jose Mourinho's washing basket trick with Chelsea all those years ago!" he joked.

As part of his sanctions, Erasmus will also miss the Nations Championship finals weekend on November 27 , with the coach prevented from entering the stadium or having direct contact with his players or management team. He will be free to return in time for the 2027 Rugby World Cup.

During the press conference, Erasmus also said he would send footage to World Rugby of the illegal tackles during his side's game against France, claiming South Africa should have had three yellow cards.

An independent panel, instructed to investigate the matter by World Rugby, said Erasmus' comments "constituted an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the match officials".

South Africa Rugby requested a full hearing in response to Erasmus' sanction and condemned online abuse World Rugby officials have received over the past week .

Jones, meanwhile, was banned for six weeks in May for criticising a match official during an U23s tour of Australia.

The Japan coach later apologised for his "inappropriate remarks", adding "I deeply regret my words and actions."

"Rassie was obviously frustrated and I can understand why," Jones said. "He's a very strong character. A deep thinker.

"Rugby needs that, but it needs respect too."

The hip-drop tackle has been a contentious issue during the Nations Championship Northern Series following it's implementation on November 1, with Ireland's Sam Prendergast being cited and later cleared for an illegal tackle on Fiji captain Peceli Yato last week.

Jones added: "Rassie had a point when he questioned some of the decisions made in his team's defeat by France, and I sent Rassie a text to that effect - he didn't reply.

"But there are appropriate and inappropriate ways to make a point and Rassie's was the latter, especially with his 'match-fixing' claim."

Erasmus has been banned twice in the past for his criticisms of referees, once for two months following the first Test of the British and Irish Lions tour to South Africa in 2021, and then again in 2022, after he published a series of X posts questioning the officiating during his side's defeat to France.

articles.title: Dan Murphy: Gloucester-Hartpury head of rugby leaves on eve of new season
articles.summary: Gloucester-Hartpury head of rugby Dan Murphy leaves the club on the eve of the new Premiership Women's Rugby season.
articles.body:
Gloucester-Hartpury head of rugby Dan Murphy has left the club on the eve of the new Premiership Women's Rugby season.

Murphy took over last season , following the departure of Sean Lynn for the Wales head coach role, and had previously spent four years with the club as scrum coach.

Three-time champions Gloucester-Hartpury finished top of the regular-season table last term but failed to reach the PWR final for the first time in four years after being beaten by Saracens in the semi-finals.

They open their 2026-27 campaign on Saturday away to Sale Sharks.

"We recognise that the timing of this change, immediately before the start of the season, is not ideal," a club statement said. , external

"However, this decision ensures stability for the squad ahead of an important first game."

Could England fears lead to fewer overseas players in PWR?

The statement added the decision was made following a "review of the programme".

"The club believes the change is in Gloucester-Hartpury's best interests," it continued.

Murphy's departure follows the exit of backs and attack coach Matt Banahan at the end of last season.

The remaining coaching team will take charge for the upcoming match, with former London Irish captain Luke Narraway joining as consultant coach while the long-term structure of the team is decided.

Gloucester-Hartpury won 14 consecutive league games in 2025-26 to storm once again to the top of the table.

However, defeats in their final two games of the campaign, before a semi-final loss to Trailfinders, meant their season ended on a muted note after a run of three championship triumphs.

They have also lost a number of influential players over the summer, including mainstays of the club as it grew into the league's dominant force in recent seasons.

England captain Zoe Stratford and fellow Red Roses centre Tatyana Heard , back-row forward Sarah Beckett and Wales hooker Kelsey Jones have all joined Saturday's opponents Sale, while Wales back-row Bethan Lewis left for Bristol.

Murphy added in a statement: "I would like to place on record my thanks to the players, staff and loyal fans for their support throughout my time at Gloucester-Hartpury.

"I wish everyone at the club all the best for the future."

articles.title: England vs New Zealand: Maro Itoje says mood in camp has changed
articles.summary: Captain Maro Itoje says a clearer sense of purpose and unity has coincided with improved performances from England this autumn.
articles.body:
Captain Maro Itoje says a clearer sense of purpose and unity has coincided with improved performances from England this autumn.

They have won their last four games, racking up victories over Fiji, Argentina, Australia and Japan in the Nations Championship.

Prior to that run, England had lost five successive Tests - a streak that included their worst ever Six Nations campaign.

They host New Zealand on Saturday, with the All Blacks stung by their first defeat by Wales in 73 years last time out.

"It feels a lot more cohesive," Itoje told BBC Rugby Union Weekly.

"It feels, from a player's point of view, that our understanding of what we're trying to do is a lot clearer.

"The level of understanding has grown from campaign to campaign and we have a very clear sense of what we're doing, what we're trying to do and we're getting into those positions a lot more effectively now."

A Times report earlier this month , external claimed senior players had sought a summit meeting with head coach Steve Borthwick after their July Nations Championship campaign due to differences of opinion over the team's direction.

Itoje was rested for that tour and Jamie George, who had reassumed the captaincy in his absence, said parts of the article were untrue and the squad were "incredibly disappointed" by its publication.

"As senior players part of our job is to challenge Steve," said George at the time. "Steve is so open to us giving feedback and having challenge."

In turn, Borthwick has credited his senior players with leading a drive on discipline that has helped England's results turn a corner.

Across their first eight Tests in 2026, England were shown 14 yellow cards and a red.

It was highlighted as a key area to improve before the autumn and they have responded with no cards and only 15 penalties conceded across their two November Tests so far.

"It's never just one thing, but I will talk about one matter," added Borthwick of the reasons behind the improvement.

"A number of weeks ago, the senior players led the players in groups. It was a big discussion topic and coming out it was a series of commitments that the players made about what they need to do.

"They've backed up those commitments in this first couple weeks. Now we know that's going be tested even more this weekend."

Itoje admitted the arrival of New Zealand brought a different atmosphere to training.

"There are weeks...and then there are weeks," he said.

"The step-up often first starts with the mind, then goes down to behaviours and actions.

"There's a sharpness needed when playing against a team like New Zealand that for other games you may not need to get to.

"Without any disrespect, when you play in New Zealand your mind has to be sharper than when you play a team like Japan."

Listen to match commentary on BBC Radio 5 Extra, BBC Sounds, BBC Sport website and through your smart speaker

Before the final round of matches and Nations Championship finals weekend, New Zealand lead the southern hemisphere standings, putting them on course for the title decider at Allianz Stadium on 29 November.

South Africa, who are a point behind in the table and could overtake the All Blacks if they slip up at Twickenham on Saturday, visit Ireland later in the day.

While Borthwick would not be drawn on Erasmus' situation or comments, he stressed the importance of respect for referees and their colleagues.

"When I first picked up a rugby ball aged 11, my schoolteacher told me, 'you call the referee sir'," he added.

"For so many years I still called the referees sir, because it's just so well ingrained. For this brilliant sport we're involved in, respect is integral. It is different to other sports and it's one of the reasons I love it."

articles.title: Wales v Australia: Flanker Jac Morgan faces Carlo Tizzano reunion in Nations Championship
articles.summary: After their controversial 2025 Lions incident, Australia flanker Carlo Tizzano is looking forward to meeting Wales' Jac Morgan in Cardiff.
articles.body:
Australia flanker Carlo Tizzano is looking forward to tackling Jac Morgan again when Wales host the Wallabies in the Nations Championship in Cardiff on Saturday.

The pair were involved in a controversial clearout incident during the British and Irish Lions' series-clinching second Test win in Melbourne in July 2025 and will face each other for the first time since.

Tizzano will test his skills against Morgan after being given the Australia number seven jersey ahead of Fraser McReight, who has been named on the replacements bench for the game at Principality Stadium.

"[Morgan] would be up there with the best open-side flankers in the world," said Tizzano.

"He is playing well for Gloucester and you want to test yourself against world-class players, and he is one of those."

Listen live on BBC Radio Wales, BBC Radio Cymru and Sports Extra on BBC Sounds

Tizzano praises Morgan's reaction to Melbourne incident

The Morgan and Tizzano collision proved the most controversial incident of the Lions' 2-1 series win in Australia in the summer of 2025.

With Australia leading 26-24 in the final minute of the match, Tizzano attempted to snatch a turnover as Lions lock James Ryan went to ground, but Morgan arrived at the ruck a split-second later and cleared him out.

In the following phase, Lions full-back Hugo Keenan went over for the winning score.

Morgan's clearout was reviewed by the television match official (TMO) and the try allowed to stand.

Australia coach at the time, Joe Schmidt, believed Morgan should have been penalised but former Lions flankers like James Haskell and Sam Warburton criticised Tizzano's reaction to the challenge, accusing him of "diving" and "simulation".

Tizzano addressed the issue last year and now declares it ancient history.

"Whatever take you have on it, it doesn't matter, the result is done, although it would have been cool to have that third game as a decider."

Schmidt rested Tizzano for the third Test in Sydney - which the Wallabies won - citing the amount of online abuse his player had received over the incident.

Tizzano praised Morgan for seeking him out after the series finale.

"Not only is he a hell of a player but he is also a good bloke," said Tizzano.

"After all that stuff happened with the Lions in game two he made an effort to say g'day and have a yarn after game three.

"He didn't have to do that and say he hoped I was all right."

Tizzano said he appreciated the way the Welshman went about his business.

"It takes a good bloke to do that. He is a proper gentleman and hopefully I will get to swap jerseys with him on the weekend, regardless of the result.

"I am keen to get that and a photo, and maybe aggravate a couple of the Lions fans!"

Australia head coach Les Kiss has since replaced Schmidt and the Wallabies are having a mixed year, suffering defeats by England and Scotland in this Nations Championship campaign.

Kiss, a former specialist defence coach, says he was impressed by Wales' 35-28 victory against New Zealand as Steve Tandy's side made a record 346 tackles.

"It became something the All Blacks couldn't work out in their own headspace," said Kiss.

"How do we beat this wonderful emotional energy, this intent, this way that was compellingly beautiful, wasn't it? There was something about it that was wonderful.

"I texted Steve [Tandy] after the game and just said that was awesome and it was pretty cool to see them do that."

Kiss says he has been impressed by Wales' development under the former Scotland and Lions assistant.

"They've had that time together and at some stage they were going to push through that threshold and click," said Kiss.

"I've coached against Wales probably eight or 10 times, they are a proud rugby nation.

"They've had tough times but at some time a game like that was going to come alive for them."

articles.title: Nations Championship: England's All Blacks acid test at Twickenham, Rassie Erasmus circus, Springboks to storm to win vs Ireland in Dublin?
articles.summary: Third week of Nations Championship Tests in northern hemisphere sees England host the All Blacks in an acid test; Ireland welcome South Africa in bonkers week Rassie Erasmus was handed six-Test ban; inaugural tournament concludes at Allianz Stadium Twickenham next weekend November 27-29
articles.body:
There is a sense of déjà vu, somewhat, for England this November when looking over their autumn performances and the general outlook emanating from them.

This time last year, England proved too strong for Australia and Fiji before welcoming New Zealand to Twickenham. In that Test, Steve Borthwick's side thrilled to a 33-19 victory over the All Blacks.

A nervy 27-23 win over Argentina followed, but England exited November buoyed by four wins, with many talking them up as a returning force in the world game, building towards Six Nations, Nations Championship and Rugby World Cup title tilts.

What followed was a disastrous Six Nations. The worst in England's history, in fact.

From five fixtures, they lost four for the first time ever, suffering defeat against Italy in a Test for the first time, as well as a record home loss to Ireland by a 42-21 margin at Twickenham.

They lost to Scotland for the fifth time in six years as the wheels well and truly came off a championship campaign which began with comfortable victory over a poor Wales side at home.

Displays in July's Nations Championship window were hardly overly positive either. A comprehensive 45-21 defeat in South Africa, a thrashing of a poor Fiji side in a Test bizarrely played in Liverpool, and holding on with 13 players to edge to victory in Argentina.

Borthwick and his players were suddenly under major pressure again, with stories of a camp rift emerging , but this month has seen 123 points scored in just two Tests - big victories over Australia and Japan.

Like last year, the All Blacks are coming to town with everyone wondering if England are back on track, or still a side short of the top table.

As such, Saturday's Test against a no-doubt angry New Zealand - following their shock defeat to Wales in Cardiff - represents something of an acid test for England.

Put on a show in victory, and talk of them as potentially one of the world's best will start to re-emerge. Suffer defeat, and criticism will filter back.

My word, it has been some week in Dublin as far as story-lines ahead of Saturday's crunch Ireland vs South Africa Test.

First, fly-half Sam Prendergast was cited for a hip-drop tackle committed against Fiji captain Peceli Yato in last week's 43-15 Ireland win - a first of its kind, with the manoeuvre outlawed at the start of this month.

Then, South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus gave the mother and father of all press conferences. Even for him - and he has quite the history - it was downright bizarre.

Off the back of the Springboks losing to France in Paris last week - clearly the reason behind Erasmus' ticking demeanour - claims and comments from South Africa's revered rugby leader ranged from extraordinary to astonishing.

He began by predicting Prendergast would get off "on a technicality" and would play in Dublin on Saturday, claiming his double Rugby World Cup-winning squad and players were treated differently at disciplinary hearings than northern hemisphere players.

Erasmus even went so far as to state "things never seem to go our way." Make of that what you will when considering he is talking about a trophy-laden side who won the last World Cup following three successive one-point knockout victories.

Far worse was to follow when Erasmus claimed "17 knee-drop tackles" by France had been missed by the referee and TMO in South Africa's defeat last week - a figure almost universally debunked when reviewed by journalists and pundits in the aftermath.

Erasmus then came out with the claims which were likely the reasoning behind World Rugby snappily handing him a six-Test suspension: questioning whether TMO's and referees were "match-fixing" and whether there was "manipulation of the game or result" of Test matches.

When a journalist at the press conference commented to Erasmus he was making a "serious intimation", his response was: "It's not an accusation."

World Rugby didn't see it that way, and though South Africa Rugby requested a formal hearing take place, Erasmus has since taken to X to confirm he will watch Saturday's Test from his Dublin hotel room and has organised a free watchalong for anyone to sign up and view him and his reaction to the Test match as it is unfolding.

The 54-year-old has now been suspended three times in five years for these sorts of incidents, which constitute "public criticism of match officials, undermining the integrity of individuals or the sport, and fuelling online abuse."

Indeed, SA Rugby have since released a statement "condemning the online abuse of officials" following confirmation of Erasmus' ban.

During the 2021 British and Irish Lions series in South Africa, after the Springboks lost the first Test, Erasmus broadcasted an hour-long critique of Australian referee Nic Berry, and was eventually handed a two-month ban from all rugby activity and 10-month matchday ban.

Berry said afterwards Erasmus' behaviour had been an "assassination of my reputation" that caused "immeasurable damage." He no longer referees Tests involving South Africa.

World Rugby found the video had contained "multiple abusive and insulting comments and attacks on the officials."

In 2022 he received a two-Test ban after sarcastic social media posts following back-to-back South Africa defeats to Ireland and France. A video critical of referee Wayne Barnes led to the official revealing he and his family had received death threats.

Outside of those punishments, Erasmus has long overseen a South Africa side and setup which has sought to find loopholes in the sport.

Against New Zealand in September and France last week, he changed his starting front-row for his replacements shortly before kick-off in clear displays of gamesmanship. In 2021, he acted as a water carrier, running onto the pitch to relay messages in-game before World Rugby changed regulations.

He has fielded 7-1 bench splits to get more heavy forwards onto the park late in Tests - something criticised as dangerous - advised his team to intentionally infringe the kick-off in order to force scrums, and is widely believed to have run a Twitter burner account called Jaco Johan for a lengthy period to criticise refereeing performances and decisions against the Boks.

Mad genius? Maybe. But increasingly a toxic figure.

Springboks to storm to victory in Dublin?

What does this all mean for the rugby on Saturday?

Well, Ireland were perhaps up against it to compete with this Springboks side in any case, but after all that has played out this week, the Springboks players are likely to come out snorting fire.

South Africa beat Ireland 24-13 this time last year , in a Test which saw Ireland shown a 20-minute red card to James Ryan and four further yellow cards, reducing them to 12 players at one point.

Two of those sin-binnings came as a result of scrum penalties, and that is likely to be an area of pain for Ireland this weekend too. The Springboks pack will be seeking utter domination in that area again.

There has also been a law tweak in terms of officiating maul defence, making it even more difficult to stop tries via the driving maul. In short, if South Africa get into Ireland's 22 with a five-metre lineout, the chances are it will result in a try.

Prendergast - whose tackle was found not to reach a red-card threshold - is back in the Ireland team at fly-half, but his form last year and earlier this year fell well below the level required, particularly in defence, but also in terms of running an attack against elite sides.

The 23-year-old has an immense task against this ultra-aggressive Springboks outfit, both in terms of leading a successful attack, and in avoiding being exposed.

If Ireland, as huge underdogs and substantially bested in terms of the power stakes, manage to win this Test, it will be one of the greatest achievements of Andy Farrell's career.

articles.title: Ireland v South Africa: Andy Farrell says refereeing is 'never going to be perfect'
articles.summary: Ireland head coach Andy Farrell says refereeing in rugby is "never going to be perfect" because it is such a complex sport.
articles.body:
Ireland head coach Andy Farrell says refereeing in rugby is "never going to be perfect" because it is such a complex sport and believes coaches have a duty to "protect the game".

Earlier this week, South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus was banned for six matches for criticising match officials, the third time he has been sanctioned for such an offence.

While Farrell did not comment specifically on Erasmus, the Ireland boss was asked why he often remains tight-lipped on officials when so many coaches across different sports air their views on refereeing standards.

"Because it [refereeing]'s tough. You're talking about football, that's easy to referee. Rugby's not," said Farrell.

"It's complex, you know. There's so many moving parts. I think it's one of the hardest sports in the world to referee so it's never going to be perfect.

"Not just that, we need to make sure that we protect the game in general as far as we want people to referee our sport coming through as well."

During an extraordinary 35-minute news conference in Dublin before Saturday's Nations Championship match with Ireland, Erasmus said that match officials had missed 17 hip-drop or knee-drop tackles in his side's loss to France last week.

Erasmus added that if television match officials (TMOs) were not intervening for reviews to limit the number of interruptions during a match then it was "manipulation".

"I'm saying if he didn't see it, it must be a technology problem. If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing?" added the two-time World Cup-winning coach.

During the news conference, Erasmus also predicted that Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast would be available to face the Springboks despite being cited for a hip-drop tackle against Fiji.

Prendergast was cleared after a panel ruled his tackle was not worthy of a red card.

Hip-drop and knee-drop tackles were outlawed before the start of the November internationals, and given the current scrutiny on officiating, Farrell was asked if extra pressure has been placed on Christophe Ridley, who will take charge of Ireland v South Africa.

"I hope not. Christophe is a top-class referee and if you know him professionally then you know he's a level-headed guy who's a very experienced referee and refereed both teams plenty of times," added Farrell.

"I think he's the perfect guy to take this on."

Hooker Sheehan named at number eight for Boks game

Divide and conquer - now maverick Erasmus plans online watchalong

Ireland fly-half Prendergast cleared to face South Africa

Farrell is hoping his side can avenge last year's 24-13 loss to the Springboks in a chaotic game in which Ireland ended the first half with 12 players on the field.

While Ireland have built towards Saturday's Test with the back-to-back world champions with victories over Argentina and Fiji, South Africa were edged out by France in an enthralling encounter at Stade de France last week.

Asked if Les Bleus showed Ireland anything different about how to beat the Boks, Farrell said: "Convert when you get the opportunity.

"If you get a few chances, that's when you need to put the points on the board because they don't give you many, but France were excellent in that regard. I think that's the bigger picture part of the game.

"We felt in the game last year, when we went down all those men and it was chaos all over the field that we still had a few opportunities that we didn't take so we have to better than that."

articles.title: Rassie Erasmus: Sky Sports understands South Africa head coach running the risk of breaching suspension with watchalong
articles.summary: Sky Sports understands Rassie Erasmus would be running risk of breaching six-Test World Rugby suspension with planned watchalong of Saturday's Ireland vs South Africa Nations Championship Test; part of Erasmus' ban covers "direct or indirect contact with team management on matchdays"
articles.body:
Erasmus is serving a six-match suspension handed down by World Rugby following extraordinary claims, saying "match-fixing" and "manipulation" was occurring in rugby after his side's defeat to France in Paris last week.

The 54-year-old was suspended for "public criticism of match officials, undermining the integrity of individuals or the sport, and fuelling online abuse", but has since taken to X to confirm he will watch Saturday's Test from his Dublin hotel room and has organised a free watchalong for anyone to sign up and view him react to the Test match as it is unfolding.

"The suspension applies with immediate effect, applies to international matches, and includes any matchday involvement including coaching, direct or indirect contact with team management or players on matchdays; entering the stadium, coaches' box, playing enclosure, technical area, approaching and/or communicating with match officials on matchday; engaging in any 'feedback' process with match officials; and engaging in media duties during the suspension."

Regarding the "direct or indirect contact with team management or players on matchdays" element of his suspension, Sky Sports sought guidance on the potential for one of South Africa's coaching staff or management set-up signing up and listening to and watching the reactions and comments of their suspended head coach during Saturday's contest - something which could have a bearing on prospective replacements and tactics in the Test.

While this specific scenario is not covered by the guidelines, Sky Sports understands Erasmus' plan could be considered a breach by rugby's governing body.

It is also understood there would be a delay to any broadcast feed Erasmus will be using.

South Africa Rugby released a statement requesting a full misconduct hearing in an immediate response to the sanction , but it is understood formal confirmation of an intention to appeal is yet to be received at World Rugby.

Erasmus has now been suspended three times in five years for these sorts of incidents.

During the 2021 British and Irish Lions series in South Africa, after the Springboks lost the first Test, Erasmus broadcasted an hour-long critique of Australian referee Nic Berry, and was eventually handed a two-month ban from all rugby activity and 10-month matchday ban.

In 2022 he received a two-Test ban after sarcastic social media posts following back-to-back South Africa defeats to Ireland and France. A video critical of referee Wayne Barnes led to the official revealing he and his family had received death threats.

On Wednesday, SA Rugby released a statement "condemning the online abuse of officials" following confirmation of Erasmus' ban.
