articles.title: Lark Atkin-Davies: England hooker sets ambitious targets on return to rugby
articles.summary: England and Bristol hooker Lark Atkin-Davies on her aims of winning a PWR title and making the Lions tour as she returns to the sport a new mum.
articles.body:
Winning a World Cup on home soil is up there among the pinnacle of things an athlete can achieve in their career.

Lark Atkin-Davies was part of the England Red Roses team that did just that in September 2025, clinching the World Cup at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham.

That match was also the hooker's final game until last month, when she returned to the pitch with Bristol following the birth of her daughter.

After achieving a goal so monumental, it would be understandable if it took some athletes a little while to find new motivation and targets going forward in their sporting career.

But for Atkin-Davies, who describes herself as a "naturally very driven and motivated person", it did not prove tricky after a year away from the sport to come back and aim for even more.

"I'd love to win a PWR (Premiership Women's Rugby) title with Bears. I've said it since being here that I think we've got everything we need to be able to do that," she told BBC Sport.

"And I truly believe that we can go and do that this season.

"Then personally, I'd love to put my hand up for selection for the Six Nations. To get back into an England shirt is a real goal of mine. And then obviously next year looking at the [British and Irish] Lions as well, I'd love to put myself in contention for that."

Could England fears lead to fewer overseas players in PWR?

'Mums thank me for changing the narrative': How motherhood in rugby has evolved

Atkin-Davies returns to rugby after birth of daughter

Atkin-Davies is one of the most experienced front-row players in England.

The 31-year-old has 74 caps and has been a mainstay of the Red Roses since making her debut in 2015.

She has also played across the PWR, starting her career at Worcester before joining Loughborough and then Bristol in 2022.

But Atkin-Davies says that before she dreamt of being a professional rugby player, she wanted to be a mother and since welcoming her daughter Olive this summer her perspective on her career has changed.

"Going through pregnancy and then having a daughter especially, has just brought this new motivation and new drive," she said.

Atkin-Davies is one of four Red Roses players who were away from the sport last season through pregnancy, with Abbie Ward, Zoe Stratford and Rosie Gallagher also welcoming children in recent months.

She has previously cited her Bristol team-mate Ward as being a huge part in showing her that rugby and motherhood can co-exist.

Lock Ward became the first centrally contracted England player to return to the sport and use the Rugby Football Union's maternity policy following the birth of her first child in 2024.

"I always speak about how much of an inspiration Abbie is and was with having Hallie (her first daughter) and then going on to win a World Cup," Atkin-Davies said.

"Seeing her with Hallie at that final whistle, carrying the World Cup around, I'd love to potentially have a moment like that.

"If Olive can grow up seeing me in an environment where I'm being challenged but where I'm doing something I love, that's a really big motivator."

Such is the regard Atkin-Davies is held in at Bristol, she has been named co-captain along with England team-mate Sarah Bern, for the new season.

After a disappointing campaign in 2025-26 when the Bears finished eighth in the table, they start away at Harlequins on Sunday, 22 November boosted further by the signing of England star Ellie Kildunne.

The Bears were beaten PWR finalists in 2024 and reached the semi-finals in 2025 but have never won the title.

Atkin-Davies believes with the squad they have, that could change this season.

"I've always truly believed that we could win the PWR title," she added.

"I said that at the beginning of the season last year - but we've got so many incredible individuals and, as a group, I just think we've always had that potential."

As for her own performances, Atkin-Davies believes the best is still to come and motherhood is to thank for that.

"Post-World Cup, as soon as I found out I was pregnant, it was like, 'OK, first and foremost, I want to make sure that I'm doing everything I can to have a really healthy pregnancy and to have Olive'," she said.

"Then also 'what can I be doing whilst I'm out of the game that can continue to keep pushing me forward?'"

She continued: "I said early on coming back to training at Bears that there's almost this new level that's been unlocked for me.

"I find that a really exciting place to be in because I think I'll be a better player for it.

"We're just at the start of the journey in terms of that return and being better than I was before."

articles.title: Scotland: McDowall goes from farm hand to captain amid Darge blow
articles.summary: Stafford McDowall was working on his dad's farm when he got the call to play for Scotland against Australia on Sunday - and six days later will be captain against Japan after Rory Darge suffered a late injury blow.
articles.body:
Stafford McDowall was working on his dad's farm when he got the call to play for Scotland against Australia on Sunday - and six days later will be captain against Japan after Rory Darge suffered a late injury blow.

It is the second change of captain head coach Gregor Townsend has had to make in a week after Sione Tuipulotu was ruled out of the Nations Championship matches against Australia and Japan.

Darge produced a man-of-the-match performance against the Wallabies in his place and the Glasgow Warriors forward was initially named again in the starting line-up despite a shoulder injury.

But, following further assessment and discussion within the Scotland camp, it has been decided he will sit out the game against Japan at Murrayfield.

Club-mate Matt Fagerson will start instead at number eight, with his place on the bench filled by Edinburgh flanker Freddy Douglas and Newcastle Red Bulls' Ollie Leatherbarrow moving forward in the back row.

Glasgow centre McDowall takes over as captain and revealed that he had returned to help out on his father's farm in Dumfries not expecting to come off the bench against the Wallabies as a second-half substitute.

Townsend on reshuffle, 'dangerous' Japan & World Cup incentive

Scotland should be grateful for Townsend - Jones

"Originally I was not involved at the weekend, not travelling reserve, so I took the opportunity to go home and help dad out," he said.

"I got there for about 12 hours, got some work done on the Saturday morning, then got the call at about 11 o'clock in the morning. Quick shower, then up the road.

"Dad wasn't too happy. I phoned him at four o'clock and asked what he was doing and he said he was doing all the jobs he had lined up for me.

"But it was awesome. Dad came up for the game the next day, so he said it worked out better than me doing jobs on the farm anyway.

"It was class. It was a bit of a whirlwind weekend."

Townsend had already made 10 changes for Japan's visit with several top players, including fly-half Finn Russell, rested before deciding not to risk Darge.

Darge will remain in the squad with the aim of being involved next week, when the Nations Championship comes to a conclusion.

Scotland are fourth in the Northern Hemisphere group and could yet be involved in a play-off for third, fifth, seventh or ninth places depending on this weekend's results.

Starting XV : Ollie Smith; Darcy Graham, Stafford McDowall (capt), Rory Hutchinson, Kyle Rowe; Tom Jordan, Jamie Dobie; Nathan McBeth, Gregor Hiddleston, Zander Fagerson, Jonny Gray, Max Williamson, Liam McConnell, Ollie Leatherbarrow, Matt Fagerson.

Replacements: Seb Stephen, Rory Sutherland, Will Hurd, Gregor Brown, Magnus Bradbury, Freddy Douglas, George Horne, Blair Kinghorn.

articles.title: Nations Championship - England 37-12 New Zealand: Most complete performance under Steve Borthwick sees hosts stay in title hunt with record win
articles.summary: Henry Slade, Jack van Poortvliet, Ben Earl, Ollie Chessum, Seb Atkinson score tries as England totally outplay New Zealand in Saturday's Nations Championship at Allianz Stadium Twickenham; Steve Borthwick's side will make final unless France beat Argentina with a bonus point in Paris
articles.body:
Last year, England picked up their first win over New Zealand for 13 years at Allianz Stadium Twickenham, but this success at the same venue was even more impressive, and leaves France needing to beat Argentina with a bonus point to stop England making the final.

Outside-centre Henry Slade, scrum-half Jack van Poortvliet, No 8 Ben Earl, blindside flanker Ollie Chessum and inside-centre Seb Atkinson scored tries as England totally dominated, racking up a record win over New Zealand.

A week on from their shock defeat to Wales in Cardiff - a first against the Welsh since 1953 - New Zealand scored two tries through prop Ethan de Groot and full-back Beauden Barrett, but the visitors were hugely disappointing in attack and at the set-piece, while they also shipped far too many penalties.

Former England World Cup winner Lewis Moody, living with motor neurone disease, emerged to stand with England's squad as they faced the haka in a unique and moving moment pre-kick-off. The home side never looked back from there.

Off early England territory, they struck for the opening try in just the fifth minute, Slade sprinting on to reach and ground a superb Fin Smith grubber-kick in behind.

Smith poorly missed the conversion, while Peter Lakai and Codie Taylor breakdown turnovers denied England a quick second.

New Zealand's first attack in the 22 saw them overthrow a lineout, however, with England soon on top again as the All Blacks kept conceding penalties.

Frustration and anxiety started to build when England proved profligate again twice more - Van Poortvliet knocking on deep in the 22 and Alex Coles held up in-goal by Tupou Vaa'i - but past the half-hour, the hosts finally had their second.

Wing Cadan Murley - into the side late after Tommy Freeman withdrew injured - made the key break from deep, with England finishing through Van Poortvliet as the scrum-half leapt and grounded on the try-line.

At 12-0, the All Blacks were virtually in need-to-score-next territory, but they soon conceded a third - albeit they could feel slightly aggrieved with the genesis of Earl's try.

With New Zealand getting over breakdown ball as England attacked in the 22, referee Nic Berry failed to reward the All Blacks with a turnover penalty, saying they had already stolen possession. As prop Fletcher Newell attempted to pass from the ruck, though, an errant boot caused a knock-on.

New Zealand should have been awarded a clearing penalty, instead, England had a scrum in the 22 and took full advantage: Earl picked from the base and charged past Damian McKenzie and Cam Roigard to score.

The All Blacks responded quickly with a close-range try through De Groot, but McKenzie missed the conversion to leave the visitors 19-5 down at the break.

Needing a markedly different second-half performance, the All Blacks lost successive lineouts early, and were then punished when Chessum finished strongly in the corner for England's fourth try - the score surviving a TMO review for a potential double-movement.

Barrett raced over for a sizzling counter-attacking All Blacks try 10 minutes later, but England extended their lead out to 15 points and three scores through a Marcus Smith penalty for offside.

With England's lineout continuing to steal New Zealand possession, and the away side intent on trying to play from deep but struggling to build up the pitch, it was the home side who scored next. Ellis Genge carried thunderously to get close, and Atkinson finished down the right.

The conversion left England 22 points ahead with 14 minutes to play, an unassailable lead the All Blacks never looked like overturning.

Genge: We were relentless - but we aren't finished article

"Off the back of a loss last week, we knew New Zealand would come out of the blocks, so it was about being relentless.

"It was no good doing it once or twice. We rode the wave well and when you go three scores up it is tough for any side.

"The reason you train so hard is to put in performances like that. We just have to keep chipping away and not get ahead of ourselves.

"We are by no means the finished article.

"I don't think anything has changed [from the Six Nations]. We have just fine-tuned it and are executing it better.

"It's not a completely different game-plan."

Itoje: I love the look of how this team is going

England captain Maro Itoje, speaking to ITV:

"It feels pretty good. I am very proud of the team, the coaches and the way we were able to pull it all together.

"I love how the team is going and look forward to the future.

"We had a fast start again and the guys coming off the bench had an unbelievable impact - but the work doesn't stop."

Next week sees the inaugural Nations Championship finals weekend, to be staged at Allianz Stadium Twickenham, over Friday November 27, Saturday 28 and Sunday 29.

Wherever each northern hemisphere nation finishes in their table decides who they will face next weekend, setting up Tests with the corresponding finishers in the southern hemisphere.

Despite victory vs the All Blacks, England are likely to finish second in their group, with France expected to beat Argentina well later on Saturday.

Should that happen, Steve Borthwick's men will face a rematch with New Zealand on Saturday November 28 (4.40pm).

For New Zealand, despite South Africa losing to Ireland Dublin, they finish second and will likely face England on Saturday November 28 (4.40pm).

articles.title: Ireland 20-17 South Africa: Springboks downed as Andy Farrell's side hold on for big victory in Nations Championship
articles.summary: Ireland hang on to seal three-point victory against South Africa on Saturday in Dublin; Springboks suffer back-to-back losses for first time since 2022 and were without head coach Rassie Erasmus after he was banned for six matches
articles.body:
The bonus point for losing within seven points of Ireland tied the Springboks with New Zealand at the top of the southern hemisphere standings, but a huge points differential separated them.

The world champion Springboks will face England or France in the final next Saturday at Twickenham but will go in with consecutive defeats for the first time in four years.

After losing to Six Nations champion France 21-19 last weekend, South Africa was expected to overpower Ireland as they did with embarrassing ease a year ago in Dublin.

But while the forwards set up both tries for South Africa, the backline attack was poor, as it was in Paris. The Springboks lost the aerial battle, struggled with Ireland's defensive line speed, and were flattered in the end to lose by only three points. The Boks led for only four minutes in the game.

They surged late into the match, with Malcolm Marx crossing on 58 minutes to set up a tense finish.

Despite a barrage of South Africa attacks, Ireland's defence was resolute, with Farrell's side moving above France to second in the northern hemisphere standings, with Les Bleus playing Argentina later on Saturday.

Farrell dubbed the victory "remarkable" and hailed his team for their performance against the world champions.

"These boys have done a lot of exceptional things over the years, but certainly in the last 12 months [this is the best]," the Ireland head coach said.

"You always want to test yourself against the best. They are world champions, and not only that, they are the world No 1, and rightly so.

"This was always a challenge we were going to look forward to, and see if we could front up. These games matter.

"The game wasn't perfect, but it was never going to be. Most of the games at the top level aren't."

O'Driscoll: 'Outstanding' Ireland the better attacking team

Former Ireland captain Brian O'Driscoll said to ITV:

"We've been treated to a number of these big days in the last 10 years in Dublin, but this one is right up there.

"I said before the game, South Africa are completely the best team in the world, with the consistency they've shown.

"Ireland today were outstanding. You have to credit Ireland rather than saying where it went wrong for South Africa.

"Ireland looked the better attacking team, and they won the battle in the air.

"We've all been querying, where are we [Ireland]? This was the litmus test and you really discover where you're at.

"With all the hype this week, they did their talking on the pitch.

"The scoreline might even have flattered South Africa. Ireland showed most of the attacking threat."

articles.title: Maro Itoje distances England from win-at-all-costs culture amid Sandpapergate fall out and Rassie Erasmus ban
articles.summary: Sandpapergate is threatening to tear Australian cricket apart; Rassie Erasmus was handed a six-game ban for an explosive rant, hitting out at officials following South Africa's defeat to France; Maro Itoje has since distanced England's rugby team from a 'win-at-all-costs' culture
articles.body:
Itoje leads England into Saturday's clash with New Zealand at Allianz Stadium , knowing victory could secure a place in the Nations Championship final on November 29.

A win against the All Blacks a year out from the World Cup final would issue a telling statement about the team's recent resurgence, but the British and Irish Lions captain believes there must be boundaries in the pursuit of success.

It comes as South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus serves a six-match ban for criticising officials during the Springboks' defeat by France last week , questioning whether the decisions they made amounted to "match fixing".

The furore surrounding repeat offender Erasmus receiving another suspension erupted while fresh accusations were made in the Sandpapergate scandal that is tearing Australian cricket apart , with Test captain Pat Cummins' role now under intense scrutiny .

"There's a line," Itoje said. "I don't believe in the metric of win-at-all costs because, depending on what that cost is, it can be extremely damaging.

"Integrity is really important. I'm Christian as well, so there are certain things which I wouldn't do.

"There's a passage in the Bible that says something along the lines of 'what does it gain for a man to gain the world but lose his soul?' Part of that is why I don't believe in that kind of thing."

Australia's win-at-all-costs mentality has been cited by some as part of the reason why Cummins' side used sandpaper to elicit more reverse swing from the ball during their 2018 tour of South Africa, with Sky Sports Cricket's Michael Atherton arguing that it created a "toxic dressing room culture".

"Don't get me wrong, I want to win. I want to do everything within my power to win," Itoje added.

"But if that power is taking performance-enhancing drugs or betting on the game, or I can list a number of other examples if that is the cost of winning, if I did those things and then win, what does the win really mean? I don't believe in that."

Erasmus, meanwhile, has now been banned three times in five years for outbursts at match officials, prompting rival head coaches such as Steve Borthwick, Eddie Jones and Fabian Galthie to call for them to be shown respect . Itoje echoes their view.

"Often in this game referees get a lot of stick," Itoje said. "It's a tough old job. They get stick because people care about the game and want the right results.

"But when you're out and talk to people from different sports - particularly footballers - what people commend rugby for is how much respect we have for the referees.

"It's really important for us as a game and a sport to make sure we continue to respect the referees.

"Some of the decisions they make will go in your favour, sometimes it'll go against you. Sometimes that's fair, sometimes that's unfair. Unfortunately, it's just the game.

"Otherwise perhaps we need to get AI to do the job, but I don't think anyone wants that either."

England have yet to decide how they will greet the haka, but Itoje insists whatever happens should only be a footnote to the afternoon.

"Our response to the haka isn't what is going to move the needle, it's what you do afterwards that matters," he added.

"What wins you the game is being really physical, incredibly accurate and really clinical against a top side like New Zealand. That's what we endeavour to do."

articles.title: Ireland v South Africa: Defiant Boks set to front up without banned Rassie Erasmus
articles.summary: South Africa prepare to face Ireland in a much-anticipated Nations Championship Test in Dublin without banned head coach Rassie Erasmus.
articles.body:
Already circled as one of the must-see fixtures in a packed November schedule, interest in the meeting between Ireland and South Africa has intensified following their contrasting disciplinary fortunes in recent days.

Not for the first time, Springboks head coach Rassie Erasmus landed himself in hot water with the powers-that-be for criticising match officials.

After receiving a six-match ban for questioning the integrity of referee Andrea Piardi and television match official Matteo Liperini in South Africa's defeat by France last week, Erasmus has been defended and condemned .

There is no doubt, however, over where the Springbok camp stand, with assistant coach Mzwandile Stick throwing his support behind Erasmus.

"He's been hands-on with our team [in the build-up], and we're in a good space," Stick said on Friday.

"Irrespective of what has happened, we love him, we appreciate him, and no-one is going to break us. I can tell you that for sure."

Erasmus also said South Africa let their country down against France, with captain Siya Kolisi bristling at a suggestion that it was a "dramatic" assessment.

"It might sound dramatic to you, but to us it means so much more," Kolisi said during his pre-match news conference.

"Rugby has done a lot for our country, and it's done a lot for many of us who come from South Africa.

"We know how happy people are and what the mood is like when we win, and when we lose, it gets tough. People care a lot about it.

"When we play, we think about the people back home. We don't take representing the country lightly because we represent every single person in South Africa when we put on that jersey."

Live on 5 Sports Extra, BBC Radio Ulster, BBC Sounds, BBC Sport website and app, with accompanying live text commentary

While Erasmus has dominated headlines this week, he will not be in attendance at Aviva Stadium on Saturday.

Instead, in a bizarre twist, the two-time World Cup winner will host a watchalong of the game from the team's Dublin hotel, with the conditions of his suspension prohibiting him from matchday contact with players and management.

Erasmus was not the only South African to receive a suspension this week with back row Jasper Wiese banned for four games for a dangerous ruck clearout against France.

While Wiese's fate did not attract the same level of scrutiny, South Africa's sense of injustice will perhaps be fuelled by the sight of Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast on Saturday.

As predicted by Erasmus , Prendergast was cleared to face the world champions after being cited for an alleged hip-drop tackle on Fiji back row Peceli Yato.

"I will tell you now for free, if that was a Fijian player tackling an Irish player with that hip-drop, that player would be in Fiji now," said Stick.

"If that was a Fijian player, he would be sitting in Fiji now doing some extra lessons of how to tackle."

Focused on erasing the pain of last year's 24-13 loss to the Springboks in Dublin, Ireland have sidestepped questions about Erasmus this week, with head coach Andy Farrell opting not to comment on his opposite number's suspension.

Irish captain Dan Sheehan said the commotion has not "affected the squad at all".

"Obviously it's a big media story for fans to get behind, but in terms of us playing the match it has zero impact," he said.

While there may be added scrutiny on referee Christophe Ridley, Sheehan said he plans to leave the official alone unless compelled to bring something "major" to his attention.

The Irish skipper has enough on his plate anyway. In addition to leading his side against the back-to-back world champions, Sheehan has been thrust into the number eight role.

The 28-year-old has won all 42 of his previous caps at hooker but moves to the back row with Caelan Doris, Jack Conan, Sean Jansen and James McNabney all ruled out.

Ireland hope Sheehan's inclusion in the back row will facilitate his powerful ball-carrying capabilities, but he insists he is not going to "overthink" it.

"I just get on with stuff. Like, eight on my back, just pick the ball up and go," said Sheehan, whose only previous start in the position was in Leinster's win over Munster last month.

"It can't be that complicated. That's my approach to it, to be honest."

Had it not been for the furore surrounding Erasmus, chances are the pre-match talk would have been dominated by scrums.

Last year, Ireland were shown five cards and conceded six penalties and a penalty try during a chastening night against the Springbok scrum.

That set-piece shellacking may have given the Irish pack nightmares over the past 12 months, and while South Africa won nine scrum penalties against France, Kolisi expects a closer contest in Dublin this time.

"Their scrum is much better than it was a year ago," he said.

"You can see they're getting penalties. But our focus is not on what they're going to do. It's about making sure we stick to our plans and do what we need to do in the scrum."

The Springboks have been boosted by the return of record cap holder Eben Etzebeth, but his second-row partner Ruan Nortje was ruled out through injury on Friday. He has been replaced by Franco Mostert, who was not originally in the matchday squad.

Ireland - who have lost their past six contests against New Zealand, France and South Africa, the three teams above them in the world rankings, by double-digit margins - have also been forced into a late change, with Thomas Clarkson replacing Sam Illo as the replacement tight-head prop.

The myriad permutations mean Ireland and South Africa could meet again in the finals weekend at Twickenham.

Either way, Saturday's sold-out contest in Dublin promises to deliver enough drama to tide fans over until next year's World Cup in Australia, where they could contest the final.

Ireland: Keenan; Baloucoune, Henshaw, McCloskey, Hansen; Prendergast, Gibson-Park; Porter, Kelleher, Furlong, McCarthy, Beirne, Baird, Van der Flier, Sheehan (capt).

Replacements: Stewart, O'Toole, Clarkson, Ryan, Timoney, Casey, Frawley, Aki.

South Africa: Willemse; Arendse, Kriel, De Allende, Hooker; Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Van den Berg; Nche, Marx, Louw, Etzebeth, Mostert, Kolisi (capt), PS du Toit, Hanekom.

Replacements: Wessels, Steenekamp, T du Toit, De Jager, De Villiers, Van Staden, Williams, Moodie.

Assistant referees: A Gardner (RA) & A Woodthorpe (RFU)

Television match official: I Tempest (RFU)

articles.title: England v New Zealand: Hosts aim to extend All Black misery
articles.summary: England's easy-on-the-eye revival will be stress-tested by a New Zealand side under sudden pressure on Saturday
articles.body:
There is a string of symbols tattooed on to Will Stuart's left foot.

A circle, two triangles, an up arrow, another circle, R1, L2, an up arrow, a triangle, and, finally L1 three times.

If you know, in this week of all weeks, you know.

England and British and Irish Lions star Stuart is indelibly, if jokingly, stamped with a Grand Theft Auto cheat code, , external which gives your character maximum in-game sex appeal.

In the absence of the injured Stuart and his cheat code at the start of this year, England certainly lost their mojo.

They had a terrible Six Nations. They were comfortably held at bay by South Africa. Five straight defeats ramped up pressure on the squad and their staff.

Stuart has now returned from a ruptured Achilles tendon and, with him, so has England's swagger.

Against Australia and Japan, England scored 20 tries.

They are ranked top of the Nations Championship for points scored and entries into the opposition 22m. Their attack has shown dexterity of a card sharp, with the sophistication of a socialite.

Those are the sort of intricacies needed to befuddle the best defences.

"We want England to support us. We want to bring joy to them," said head coach Steve Borthwick this week.

So far, this autumn, that objective has been achieved. Twickenham has been seduced by two charismatic displays which have been high on entertainment, if low on jeopardy.

New Zealand are sore. Last weekend's defeat by Wales - their first in 73 years - stung. Coach Dave Rennie's public accusation that the players had "let the country down" will have salted wounds.

He may well have said the same of the insipid performance the team put up in a 33-19 defeat by England last year, under his predecessor Scott Robertson.

The Rennie-ssance overseen by their new boss, with wins over France, Ireland and South Africa in his first few months in charge, has given way to talk of looming crisis.

All Black backs are up hard against a brick wall. And big names - Will Jordan, Jordie Barrett, Cam Roigard and Damian McKenzie - are back to blast their way out of a hole.

England have had their fun over the past couple of weeks.

One of the benefits of being in the northern half of the Nations Championship is a steadier supply of fodder.

Fiji and Japan - the two teams invited to fill out the southern half of the new competition - have won only one of 10 games between them and have a combined points difference of minus 257.

Despite last week's reverse, New Zealand - along with world champions South Africa - are where southern-hemisphere quality is concentrated. And where England's revival will be truly stress-tested.

The comeback of Stuart, and others, has been key for England.

England made a clean sweep of their last autumn campaign, with a high-calibre set of replacements key.

Any lingering final-quarter hopes for the visitors were flushed out by England's depth on the bench.

Stuart is playing the front-row super-sub once again. Fin Baxter - another long-time injury absentee - starts at loosehead, to allow England to rotate between two top-class front rows.

George Martin - an old-school second row enforcer who is recently back from his own 14-month lay-off - is on a bench, also including Henry Pollock and Marcus Smith, loaded with stardust and points to prove.

George Furbank, whose running threat and playmaking ability from deep adds an extra dimension to attack, starts at full-back after a rotten run of knocks and set-backs.

Captain Maro Itoje seems rejuvenated by a summer off. Ollie Chessum is perhaps in the best form of his life. Seb Atkinson - still only eight caps into his Test career - has brought a mix of hard running and soft skills to 12.

Will Joseph's pace, power, good form and ability to play in midfield, as well as on the wing, has thrust him right into Rugby World Cup reckoning.

England aren't at full strength. Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, Tom Curry and Alex Mitchell are big misses. Sam Underhill and Guy Pepper too.

But injuries are inevitable. And England, at the moment, are relatively fully loaded.

"The last time we had this depth was a year ago," Borthwick said, drawing an implicit link back to England's purple patch of 12 straight wins through 2025 and the very start of 2026.

The mood music, like the performances, has been good.

Itoje suggested there was a renewed sense of purpose and ownership in camp. Borthwick credited the players with leading a successful drive to improve discipline.

Attack coach Lee Blackett's fingerprints are all over some of the attacking shapes thrown over the past fortnight.

Victory over New Zealand, of any kind, would stomp the accelerator to the floor.

If it comes with eye candy, all the better.

articles.title: Tomos Williams believes Wales' stars gain confidence playing in Prem
articles.summary: Exposure to the English Prem has boosted the confidence of Wales' players, says scrum-half Tomos Williams.
articles.body:
Exposure to English rugby's Prem has boosted the confidence of Wales' top players, says scrum-half Tomos Williams.

The 31-year-old is among nine England-based players in Steve Tandy's Wales team to face Australia on Saturday, including the entire front row.

Earlier this month, Tandy named a record 12 players in his match-day squad who were based outside of Wales. In the last World Cup, that figure was just six in the entire squad.

Tandy, who spent six years coaching with Scotland, said he was excited at having so many players experiencing different competition.

Saracens half-back Williams said playing in England has helped changed the mindset of Welsh players after years of struggling for their regions and country.

"The biggest thing I found when I moved to England was that the English boys are a lot different to the Welsh boys, a lot more confident than us," he said.

"We probably get that confidence being there and experiencing those environments. Boys realise that they're not a million miles better than us.

"You can probably see that in some of the boys that have just gone over, Waino [Aaron Wainwright], Dewi [Lake] and Jac [Morgan]."

Listen live on BBC Radio Wales, BBC Radio Cymru and Sports Extra on BBC Sounds

Morgan, who left Ospreys along with Lake in the summer, said he had added an extra attacking dimension to his game by moving to Gloucester and was named Prem player of the month in October.

Louis Rees-Zammit (Bristol), Max Llewellyn (Gloucester), Nicky Smith (Sale), Archie Griffin (Bath) and Dafydd Jenkins (Exeter) will also start against the Wallabies in Cardiff with Kane James (Exeter) among the replacements and set for his first home Test appearance.

Rhys Carre (Saracens), Louis Hennessey (Bath) and Gabriel Hamer-Webb (Leicester) have also featured this month as well as Adam Beard (Montpellier).

Little wonder then that the Welsh Rugby Union has approached the Rugby Football Union over the creation of an Anglo-Welsh league.

Flanker Tizzano looks forward to Morgan reunion

Wales reveal reasons for leaving out Botham

Player confidence was clear to see last weekend when Wales claimed a historic victory over New Zealand.

While Wales may have stunned the rugby world by ending a 73-year-wait to beat the All Blacks again, Williams insisted the team had always believed.

"Winning games, that's what you strive for, that's why we play sport," he said.

"It's fine for other people to be surprised that we won, but hopefully we shouldn't be too surprised.

"You wouldn't be setting foot on the pitch at this level if you didn't back yourself to win."

Williams is now one of just seven Wales players to have beaten all three southern hemisphere giants - New Zealand, Australia and South Africa.

But while the British and Irish Lion admitted Saturday's result was the most emotional he had been involved in, he shrugged off the significance almost as casually as he did Saturday's win.

"It was class, we enjoyed it but you've got to move on pretty quickly," he said.

"Hopefully we'll do it again [beat the All Blacks] and it won't stick out too much."

Wales head coach Tandy certainly did not hold back on his praise for the "outstanding" Williams.

"His passing game when attacking inside the 30-metre zone is right up there with the best in world rugby," said Tandy.

"He's driven the team brilliantly over the last two weeks, both in matches and in training. Alongside Dewi and Jac he plays a massive leadership role and his belief rubs off on the entire squad."

A wounded Wallabies side after their loss in Scotland are the next challenge, with Wales looking to complete a Cardiff hat-trick against Les Kiss' side.

And Williams is more than aware that reality can hit back hard.

"Australia are a good team and they'll be firing Saturday," he said.

"They haven't had the results they've wanted to over the last couple of games, so I reckon they'll be well up for it.

"We've got to get our heads around that, park that [All Blacks] game now, and be ready for Saturday."

articles.title: Wales v Australia: Welsh heroes aim to back up historic All Blacks win
articles.summary: Wales must kick on when they host Australia in the Nations Championship on Saturday, fresh from making history against New Zealand.
articles.body:
The Australia fixture was meant to be Wales' big shot.

It was the chance to finally claim the scalp of a southern hemisphere big gun. The opportunity to make a statement ahead of the 2027 World Cup that they are capable of beating any of the top teams on their day.

But Steve Tandy's side went seven days early.

Wales will now attempt to claim a hat-trick of Cardiff wins in the Nations Championship on Saturday night after the most unlikely of victories against New Zealand.

It is a success that has changed the November narrative. Rather than "can they do it?", the question is now "can they back it up?".

Listen live on BBC Radio Wales, BBC Radio Cymru and Sports Extra on BBC Sounds

Wales' win against the All Blacks was arguably the biggest shock in international rugby since Japan beat South Africa in Brighton in the 2015 World Cup.

What is rarely mentioned is that the Brave Blossoms - hindered by a farcical four-day turnaround - failed to back that up when thumped by Scotland in Gloucester in their following game.

Japan caused another surprise on home soil in 2019 when they beat Ireland and that time they did follow up with victories against Samoa and Scotland.

"It's a real test of our mental and physical preparation," admitted head coach Tandy.

"We can't assume that because one scoreboard went our way, everything is fixed.

"We have to double-down on performance, how we recover, how we train and executing the core areas of our game.

"We have to be at our absolute best to compete with the Aussies."

Tandy frequently talks about performance rather than results, yet this is an occasion where an ugly victory would do.

Wales' belief has soared but they remain slight underdogs for the fixture.

The odds are not as generous as last week's 20-1, but Tandy's men are hunting another scalp.

They are ninth in the world rankings and the Wallabies are seventh.

"It's not do or die, but they will want the performance and result," former Wales hooker Scott Baldwin told the Scrum V podcast.

"None of us expected the New Zealand win, it was one for the ages. If they perform anywhere near that then they win quite comfortably.

"After you have beaten the All Blacks, you go into the Six Nations believing you can beat anyone."

Flanker Tizzano looks forward to Morgan reunion

Tandy thanks 'amazing' family after All Blacks win

Wales enjoyed their moment, dealt with the acclaim, soaked in the social media reactions and fulfilled plenty of extra media requests.

But they were back in for training on Monday afternoon - business as usual(ish).

"I don't think anyone really felt a sore body until Tuesday because of the emotion and riding the weekend," said captain Dewi Lake.

"I have no doubt the boys will be ready to go.

"There might have been some things the coaches pulled here and there, some minutes off the clock, but the intensity, the challenge, the effort has been exactly the same.

"We've spoken about kicking on from this and to do that you just have to keep pushing."

Wales can go three from three in Cardiff and would then travel to London hunting a perfect November in a fixture likely to be against Japan.

Warren Gatland's class of 2018 are the only team to have enjoyed an autumn clean sweep.

Wales do not want to go from the biggest of highs against New Zealand - something that even the Grand Slam greats could not achieve - to a deflating home loss.

"When you come down off a high like that it is important you get the messaging right," said Gloucester hooker Lake.

"Steve, the coaches and other leaders have really delivered that this week in terms of it being an opportunity for us to build rather than it just being a one-off game we performed in that people will remember forever - but then we didn't turn up the week after.

"There are two ways we can go, we kick on or it's back to how we were. It's an opportunity to kick on."

The Wales players have had an extra day of recovery than the Wallabies, who lost to Scotland on Sunday, but Tandy's men did have a considerably bigger defensive effort and high ball-in-play time.

Wales used plenty of emotional and physical energy, leading to the management team freshening up their starting line-up.

They have gone back to the same XV that faced Japan a fortnight ago , and the pressure is on the returnees.

Blind-side flanker Alex Mann has been a favourite of Tandy's – starting in 12 of 14 Tests - but must now respond to Cardiff club-mate James Botham's excellence.

Lock Ben Carter got ahead of Adam Beard in the Six Nations but was tasked with providing energy off the bench last week.

The Dragons co-captain gets back in courtesy of Beard suffering a minor shoulder issue and must deliver when calling at the line-out after an off-day against Japan.

Wing Josh Adams, who was rested, and number eight Aaron Wainwright, back from a leg injury, have nothing to prove on the Test stage but would not be human if they were not a little disappointed to have missed out on making history.

Back row Taine Basham and wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb go from the starting line-up to missing out, with Kane James given the role of impact sub.

The promising Exeter flanker is set for a first international appearance in Cardiff after winning his first cap in Argentina in July.

"We have fresh and hungry players coming in, which will add the energy that we need," said Tandy.

Eleven Wales players are set for their third start on the spin, with the coaching staff poised to rotate for Twickenham.

While Wales are hunting an autumn clean sweep, Australia are at risk of another November whitewash.

The last time that the Wallabies won in Europe was the 52-20 win in Cardiff two years ago.

They have suffered eight successive losses on this continent since that eight-try victory and travel to Cardiff fresh from a heavy defeat by England and a loss to Scotland in a drab encounter.

"Australia are there for the taking," said former Wales centre Shanklin on the Scrum V podcast.

"I have been a little bit disappointed with how they are playing. They haven't looked that good, they look lost in attack."

The Wallabies could drop to ninth in the world rankings on Monday, although that would take a heavy loss at Principality Stadium.

Les Kiss' side have enjoyed some notable results this year - a superb win against South Africa in Perth plus a win and a draw in Argentina - and remain slight favourites.

"A hurting team is a dangerous team. We've been in that position, and probably still are to an extent," said Lake.

"We know they're a dangerous team and they've got dangerous players. Look back over the last 12 months and they've had some big results and big performances."

An unfriendly kick-off time for the Wallabies fixture presented a challenge to the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU), but then Lake and his team ensured a ticket surge.

A crowd of 55,152 witnessed history against New Zealand at the 74,000-capacity Principality Stadium - but the 62,000 mark has already been passed for Australia.

"Our performance drives people to come and watch us and get behind us," said Lake.

"We saw that in spades last Saturday for every try and the defensive shifts. I think the loudest cheer was for a held-up ball or Eddie James and Louis Rees-Zammit's tackle [of a New Zealander] into touch in the 77th minute.

"That's what drives us on the field as well. The energy that we get from the crowd does help massively and our performance drives that, it's not shock that the two go hand in hand.

"We've seen how it's kind of given the nation a bit of hope. We've seen loads of videos rolling in, and that hope drives us as well."

A win against Australia would not prompt tears of joy in the stands, but Wales want to celebrate again after so much post-World Cup pain.

Wales will not mathematically know their Twickenham opponents before kick-off against the Wallabies, but they could be 99% certain to finish fifth.

If Scotland win with a bonus point against Japan then Tandy's side would need to do likewise, and win by 20 points more than the Scots.

Wales cannot drop to sixth and are likely to finish fifth, and that will mean another meeting with Japan unless Fiji win in Italy with a bonus point.

The Fijians would also need to turn around a hefty points difference gap to the Brave Blossoms.

The game between the fifth-placed teams is on Saturday, 28 November (13:10 GMT), followed in the double-header by the nations that finish second in the respective southern and northern tables.

articles.title: England vs New Zealand: Maro Itoje says Lewis Moody gave team 'lift' as former captain joins side to face Haka
articles.summary: Lewis Moody was invited onto the field to join England to face the Haka during England's 37-12 victory against New Zealand on Saturday; Maro Itoje said Moody's presence 'lifted' his team; Moody was diagnosed with MND in 2025 and is campaigning to raise awareness of the illness
articles.body:
As the All Blacks prepared to perform the Haka, Itoje wandered to the touchline and welcomed Moody, who was diagnosed with Motor Neurone Disease (MND) in September 2025, onto the field.

The 48-year-old, who won 71 caps for England, took up position at the point of England's arrow formation to accept the challenge from the All Blacks during Saturday's match.

After the Haka, the England team all embraced Moody.

It was an emotional start to the match but Itoje believed having the "inspirational" former flanker on the pitch gave England a "lift".

"I got into playing rugby relatively late in comparison to a lot of my colleagues and I remember watching England play, particularly around 2011," Itoje said during his press conference.

"Lewis is such an inspirational man, he was an inspirational player and given his diagnosis, the players jumped at the opportunity to support him.

"He and his family gave us that extra lift today."

England subsequently got off to a flying start, with Henry Slade collecting a grubber kick from Fin Smith inside four minutes of kick-off to give England an early lead.

Moody had presented the England side with matchday jerseys at their Pennyhill Park base on Friday night.

"He came to spend some time with us yesterday," Itoje said.

"He presented us our shirts for today's game, he spoke to us, addressed us, and there's no doubt that his presence, him joining us for the Haka, him spending time with us, gave us an extra lift."

All of England's players wore specially customised boots that had the logo of Moody's 'Front Up to MND' campaign printed on them.

England players also signed and donated their warm-up tops and match jerseys.

Itoje said Rugby Football Union chief executive Bill Sweeney called him a few weeks ago to discuss the idea about having the former British and Irish Lion join England for the Haka. The team fully supported the idea.

"I just remember his heroic performances for England, throwing his body in and around the team, and the way he played was inspirational," Itoje said.

"He was one of the guys that I looked up to as a young boy playing rugby.

"I have the honour and privilege of captaining this great team, and to be able to welcome him, to be able to receive him onto the field is a memory that's going to live with me for the rest of my life.

"As the England group, there are many players who've been particularly pertinent in supporting him, but just as an England group, we're just so proud to be able to support him and help him, and going forward, whatever we can do to help him and his family, we would love to."

After the match, Steve Borthwick said he was buoyed by his side's performance but added he felt England had left points out there, after struggling to take chances when breaking into the All Blacks' 22.

Jack van Poortvliet, Ben Earl, Ollie Chessum all touched down in the first half, before Ollie Chessum and Seb Atkinson followed up with second-half tries.

"The first half today, there were chances we didn't take; we had a lot of entries into their 22 that ended up with us not scoring," said Borthwick. "That's credit to New Zealand, that's not just us.

"There's a team there trying to stop you, and they did really well. I thought their breakdown pressure was excellent; their counter-rucking was very good.

"We ended up with ball that was too slow.

"Later on we took our opportunities much more quickly and better, and restricted New Zealand's opportunity to try and take our breakdown ball.

"There was an adjustment the players made. Our carrying was better in the second half and the bench really had a big impact on that. That was evident."

Fin Smith ran the show against the All Blacks on Saturday, but concerns began to mount after the England No 10 was seen putting ice on his legs after being substituted.

Borthwick confirmed Smith had suffered cramp in both legs and was hopeful that he would recover.

"I'd anticipate that he recovers quite quickly," he said.

Tommy Freeman pulled up with a quad issue before the match and Borthwick was uncertain about whether the winger could play next week.

"Tommy Freeman, we don't know," Borthwick said.

"We're hopeful, so there's a niggle in his quad; maybe there's a chance [he can play] next week.

"It's probably too early to say that right now.

"Hopefully that's not anything longstanding but we can't be any more precise than that at this stage."

After suffering back-to-back defeats to both England and Wales, questions are now mounting over New Zealand's form.

They made costly errors in key areas on Saturday, with Earl running through the All Blacks backline to score off the back of a scrum after the visitors conceded a knock-on.

The All Blacks conceded eight penalties inside their own half and head coach Dave Rennie didn't hold back in his assessment.

"We were just miles off tonight," Rennie said.

"[We] lacked the intensity and accuracy to be competitive at this level, weren't very good.

"We had a 30-odd per cent position, 30-odd territory, and turned over 2-1 to them, so just gave them too many opportunities down our end to hurt us, and just couldn't get any continuity going at our end."

articles.title: Lewis Moody: Ex-captain joins England side to face New Zealand's haka before Nations Championship match
articles.summary: Former England captain Lewis Moody joins the current team to face New Zealand's haka in an emotional start to Saturday's Test match at Allianz Stadium.
articles.body:
Former England captain Lewis Moody joined the current team to face New Zealand's haka in an emotional start to Saturday's Test match at Allianz Stadium.

Moody, who was diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND) last year, stood at the centre of England's line-up - between captain Maro Itoje and one of the team's vice-captains, Ellis Genge - as they faced up to the traditional pre-match challenge.

Led by Genge's fellow vice-captains Ollie Chessum and Jamie George, England then advanced to form a V shape, similar to the formation they took before last year's victory and the 2019 Rugby World Cup semi-final win against the All Blacks.

Moody, who was embraced by most of England's team in the aftermath of the challenge and its acceptance, also delivered the match ball.

Superb England run up record win over New Zealand

England stars to help launch Moody MND challenge at All Blacks match

With Twickenham energised, England started the match fast, with Henry Slade getting on the end of a Fin Smith grubber kick to score the first try after just four minutes.

They went on to win 37-12, which was a record margin of victory for England over New Zealand.

England coach Steve Borthwick told BBC Radio 5 Live: "It was particularly significant. What was really powerful was Lewis did the shirt presentations last night and he spoke unbelievably in the way he put his message across and it really resonated with the players.

"It was some way to start a big game of rugby."

All of England's players wore boots emblazoned with the logo of Moody's Front Up to MND campaign, to which signed warm-up and match-worn shirts will be donated.

The campaign's first fundraising drive is a mass-participation coastal walk in June, which aims to raise more than £1m to fund research into the disease.

A statement from England Rugby said: "As a hugely respected former England captain, it was important to the England men's team to show their support for Lewis and to involve him in many areas of the match day, including on the pitch.

"Supporting Lewis and Front Up reflects the game's commitment to standing alongside those affected by MND, and to help raise awareness and funds for research."

Moody delivered the match ball before England's victory over Australia last autumn, a few weeks after he revealed his diagnosis in an interview with BBC Breakfast.

Last weekend, Wales players were bathed in red light and smoke during the All Blacks' haka in a response that was 'a year in the making'.

articles.title: England 37-12 New Zealand: Hosts run up record win over All Blacks
articles.summary: England's revival roars up a gear as they beat New Zealand by a record margin after former captain Lewis Moody leads the hosts' response to the haka.
articles.body:
Tries: Slade, Van Poortvliet, Earl, Chessum, Atkinson Cons: F Smith (2), M Smith Pens: M Smith (2)

Tries: De Groot, B Barrett Cons: McKenzie

England's revival roared up a gear as they beat New Zealand by a record margin after former captain Lewis Moody led the hosts' response to the haka.

Moody, who was diagnosed with motor neurone disease last year, stood at the centre of a flying V formation that England had adopted for their victories over the same opponents last year and in the 2019 Rugby World Cup semi-final.

In terms of margin, this win trumped both - and the other seven England victories in the teams' 121-year rivalry.

And the hosts were full value for it. They dominated the All Blacks from the start.

Henry Slade crossed for the opening try in the fourth minute and only England's own mistakes prevented them taking a bigger lead than their 19-5 advantage into the break.

Beauden Barrett marked his 150th Test appearance by rounding off a coast-to-coast Kiwi try to cut England's advantage to 24-12. But his team never really threatened to reel in Steve Borthwick's men.

England introduced five forwards off the bench in the immediate aftermath of that 55th-minute score and, with Ellis Genge in fearsome carrying form, they had more than enough to see out victory in comfort.

Seb Atkinson took a delayed pop pass from Marcus Smith to stroll in for England's fifth try just after the hour.

The hosts finished the game camped down in the New Zealand 22m in search of a sixth score while choruses of Swing Low rolled around the stands.

For New Zealand, who suffered a shock defeat by Wales last weekend, it is a result that suggests a long Test season, which included four Tests against South Africa, may be catching up with them.

By contrast England, who could still end up in next weekend's Nations Championship grand final depending on results, are riding a wave of confidence.

Ex-captain Moody joins England in emotional haka response

Moody's involvement in the pre-match challenge ensured New Zealand were met by a wall of noise and relentless pressure from kick-off.

Fast starts have become a feature of England's autumn campaign so far, with Australia and Japan both blitzed in the opening minutes.

New Zealand are a class above those teams, but fared little better against the revved-up hosts.

The game was only four minutes old when Slade, with roars from the stands at his back, won the race to a Fin Smith grubber.

After that initial strike, England maintained a stranglehold on the match.

A brilliant 50:22 from George Furbank bought more territory and England, hitting hard in defence, penned New Zealand back.

Their dominance did not immediately translate into points.

Individual errors - Jack van Poortvliet's fumble at the back of a breakdown, Fin Smith's over-cooked cross-field kick, Alex Coles being held up over the line - meant chances went begging.

After half an hour, England had enjoyed 74% of possession, 82% of territory and made 183 metres to New Zealand's 34. A sense the hosts may ultimately regret those mistakes nagged at fans in the stands.

It proved misplaced. Van Poortvliet plunged over from short range after a Cadan Murley break and then, four minutes later, the excellent Ben Earl thundered off the back of a scrum, trampled through Cam Roigard and went under the posts.

New Zealand prop Ethan de Groot burrowed over to repair some of the damage, but at 19-5 down at the break, the visitors were both reeling and somewhat fortunate to still be in touch.

England started the second half at the same breathless pace that marked their approach to the first. Ollie Chessum, lurking out wide, ploughed through the unfortunate Will Jordan for a try inside two minutes of the restart.

Beauden Barrett's score briefly had the embers glowing for New Zealand, but England's bench stomped out any hopes of a comeback.

Genge, Will Stuart, Luke Cowan-Dickie, George Martin and Greg Fisilau gave the forward brought crunching physicality and line speed.

The starters were not far behind, with Chessum levelling former All Black captain Scott Barrett with a superb tackle.

With victory long since secured, an 81,953-strong crowd could relish those individual duels, reflect on a scoreline that exceeded the famous 2012 win and look forward to next weekend, and a possible rematch with New Zealand or meeting with South Africa, at leisure.

articles.title: Nations Championship: Liam McConnell shines as 11-try Scotland dismantle Japan
articles.summary: A Liam McConnell hat-trick inspires Scotland in an 11-try Nations Championship rout of Japan at Murrayfield.
articles.body:
Tries: Graham 3, McConnell 3, Rowe, Smith 2, Dobie, Hutchinson Cons: Jordan 4, Horne 2

A Liam McConnell hat-trick in only his third appearance inspired Scotland in an 11-try Nations Championship rout of Japan at Murrayfield.

The 22-year-old Edinburgh back row was electrifying, not just in scoring three wonderful tries, but on both sides of the ball, attack and defence.

The sparkling Darcy Graham also got a hat-trick - his 39th, 40th and 41st international tries - against Eddie Jones' severely weakened team, blasted to kingdom come by England last weekend, and now on the end of another bruising experience.

They shipped five tries in an opening half that ended with the Scots leading 29-0. Game over. Graham got two of his in that opening spell with McConnell getting his first, with Kyle Rowe and Ollie Smith adding the others.

There's been considerable buzz about McConnell for a long time now and significant frustration among his supporters at his lack of opportunities with Scotland. He got his second and third scores before the hour. Jamie Dobie added a seventh.

Graham & McConnell score hat-tricks as Scotland thrash Japan - reaction & as it happened

Gregor Townsend changed most of his team from the win over the Wallabies last Sunday but the second string, if you can call them that, were at it right from the start.

Dobie's box-kick was spilled by the visitors and the last person they would have wanted to seize on the loose ball was Graham. He hacked on and scored. Tom Jordan, playing 10 instead of Finn Russell, was errant off the tee for much of the day and missed the first of his conversions. George Horne came on later and banged over some extras.

Scotland never relented in the building of their points mountain. Kyle Rowe took the ball in the air and the appreciation of space and speed of execution was too much for Japan after that.

Smith, heavily influential at full-back, was at the heart of so many things and he linked with Graham to put McConnell away. The big back row with his giant stride and his fantastic pace ate up the ground to score.

Rowe scored the third after brilliant running from Graham. Barely a quarter of the Test gone and it was already 17-0. Graham's solo score, following a sumptuous pick-up off the floor, brought up the bonus point just after the hour. The wing sped away to score under the posts.

Japan were reeling at the accuracy and the ambition of the Scotland attack. Getting cut open repeatedly, they had no answers. A fifth try arrived just before the break when Japan kicked, rather unwisely and aimlessly, out of defence - just meat and drink to Scotland.

McConnell's outstanding running put the hosts on the front foot and Japan in the horrors. Dobie and Rory Hutchinson set up Smith in the corner.

You felt for Japan. Rabbits in the headlights. McConnell's second came via more thrilling stuff from Darcy who picked up, chipped ahead and gathered to get in behind Japan. He offloaded to the rapid flanker who sprinted in from distance.

A form of Japanese consolation came when full-back Takuro Matsunaga scored but the Scottish response was swift and brutal. McConnell again, of course. He won the ball in the air and flew away to glory. A statement performance albeit against a broken team.

Dobie got the next after nice work from the quietly impressive Hutchinson and Smith got his second and Scotland's ninth after Blair Kinghorn had entered the fray with impact.

The last thing on earth that Japan needed was two yellow cards in the last 10 minutes but that's what they got.

Hutchinson scored not long after it became 15 versus 14 and Graham completed his own hat-trick when it was 15 versus 13.

A savage day for Japan but an unforgettable experience for the hat-trick men - especially the serial-scorer Graham and the emerging star McConnell. His smile at the end was so bright it could have powered half the city's electricity for the night.

Scotland rout Japan at Murrayfield in the Nations Championships

articles.title: Scotland 67-5 Japan: Captain Stafford McDowall delighted with win
articles.summary: Stand-in captain Stafford McDowall praises Scotland for keeping their "foot on the throat" of opponents Japan in their thumping 67-5 Nations Championship win.
articles.body:
Stand-in captain Stafford McDowall praised Scotland for keeping their "foot on the throat" of opponents Japan in their thumping 67-5 Nations Championship win at Murrayfield.

After a disappointing defeat by New Zealand to start their autumn campaign, Gregor Townsend's side responded with a gritty victory against Australia last weekend and built on that performance against a depleted Japan outfit.

They led 29-0 at half-time, before going through the gears in the second half.

Eleven tries, including hat-tricks from winger Darcy Graham and effervescent young flanker Liam McConnell, boosted Scotland's chances of finishing third in the Northern Hemisphere table.

The Scots will likely face either Argentina or Australia in their competition finale next weekend, depending on results elsewhere on Saturday.

McConnell shines as 11-try Scotland dismantle Japan

Graham & McConnell score hat-tricks as Scotland thrash Japan - reaction & as it happened

"We got off to a good start, which helped settle a few of the boys' nerves," said McDowall, who led the team in the absence of Sione Tuipulotu and Rory Darge.

"We had a chat on the pitch before we went in at half-time saying we didn't want to let the game fizzle out and I'm most proud of the fact we kept our foot on the throat in the second half. The boys that came off the bench did really well.

"I think it's a big step for this group and hopefully it's enough to bump us up the table. We are looking forward to the Six Nations and all those northern hemisphere teams are going to want to finish on a positive note."

While McConnell took the headlines for his try-scoring exploits, head coach Townsend was keen to highlight the work of the entire back row.

"Matt Fagerson went through a lot of work and hopefully his injury isn't serious. Ollie Leatherbarrow was great on both sides of the ball and Liam [McConnell] stands out for his tries."

Graham extended his lead as Scotland's record try scorer with his 39th, 40th and 41st international scores and, given the need to win handsomely in order to increase their points difference, Townsend was delighted with his team's execution.

"Japan were tough opposition. I know the scoreline doesn't suggest that, but it took a number of phases, really good focus at the breakdown, really smart decision-making to score in the first half," he said.

"The pressure told. The work we did in the first half not only got points on the board, but put pressure on Japan.

"Obviously we had an eye on that points total and getting to that number of points was an ambition and they delivered on that."

Scotland rout Japan at Murrayfield in the Nations Championships

articles.title: Ireland 20-17 South Africa: Irish edge past world champions in Nations Championship thriller
articles.summary: Ireland exact revenge on world champions South Africa with a thrilling win in Dublin after England's victory over New Zealand dashes Andy Farrell's side's hopes of reaching next weekend's Nations Championship final.
articles.body:
Tries: Baloucoune 2, Kelleher Con: Prendergast Pen: Prendergast

Try: Van den Berg, Marx Cons: Feinberg-Mngomezulu 2 Pens: Feinberg-Mngomezulu

Ireland exacted revenge on world champions South Africa with a thrilling win in Dublin after England's victory over New Zealand dashed Andy Farrell's side's hopes of reaching next weekend's Nations Championship final.

With banned South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus hosting a watchalong stream from his team's hotel, the Springboks fell to back-to-back Test defeats for the first time since November 2022 after last week's loss to France in Paris.

A losing bonus-point, however, is enough for South Africa to top the southern hemisphere table and secure a place in the final against England or France, who face Argentina on Saturday night (20:10 GMT).

Ireland, who were shown five cards during last year's 24-13 loss to the Springboks in Dublin, led at the break after two tries from Robert Baloucoune and a Ronan Kelleher score, with Morne van den Berg crossing for the visitors.

After Canan Moodie had a try ruled out early in the second half, Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast - who was cleared to play by a disciplinary panel earlier this week - stretched Ireland's lead with a penalty.

However, hooker Malcolm Marx's 57th-minute try hauled South Africa back into it before yellow cards for Ireland captain Dan Sheehan and Springbok replacement Marco van Staden - the latter upgraded to red - set up a nail-biting denouement in the final 10 minutes.

But amid a hair-raising atmosphere inside Aviva Stadium, Ireland held on for a much-needed win after six successive double-digit defeats by the Springboks, New Zealand and France.

Victory moves Ireland into second before France's meeting with Argentina in Paris.

Nations Championship - Ireland condemn South Africa to back-to-back defeats

Ireland front up to SA after Erasmus-dominated build-up

After an explosive build-up headlined by Erasmus, who was banned for six matches on Tuesday after questioning the integrity of match officials in last week's game against France, Saturday's contest in Dublin had a lot to live up to.

But it delivered emphatically during a breathless first half as Ireland fronted up impressively to South Africa's immense physicality.

In last year's meeting in Dublin, Ireland ended a nightmarish first half with 12 players on the field as South Africa - and their mighty scrum - played the game on their terms.

Fuelled by the pain of that encounter, Ireland attacked the game with real gusto and while South Africa fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu kicked the first points of the game, Ireland bossed possession and territory for much of the opening half.

There were plenty of moments for the sold-out crowd to cheer, with perhaps the biggest roar reserved for the hosts winning a rare scrum penalty after 26 minutes.

Baloucoune was exceptional, too. In addition to faring well in the aerial battle, the rapid Ulster wing displayed his finishing skills to get Ireland on the board, slipping past Damian Willemse and touching down after being picked out by Stuart McCloskey.

While Baloucoune - who also crossed twice against Fiji last week - was denied a second try by a superb piece of last-ditch defending by Springbok number eight Cameron Hanekom, Joe McCarthy won a turnover to deny the visitors momentum.

From there, Ireland kicked to the corner and eventually worked the ball back to Baloucoune on the right, who dived over in the corner for his second.

But with both conversion attempts missed by Prendergast, Ireland were pegged back when South Africa won a penalty inside green territory, with Van den Berg dotting down off the back of a scrum.

Unlike last year, though, Ireland had the final say of the half and restored their lead when Kelleher scored off a well-worked line-out.

South Africa's frustration deepened early in the second half when Moodie's fine finish in the corner was ruled out after the replacement back was pushed into touch by Mack Hansen.

Ireland pulled further clear when Prendergast atoned for his missed kicks at goal with a penalty to put the hosts 20-10 up.

But after world player of the year Marx forced his way over with more than 20 minutes remaining, Ireland were denied a fourth try when Sheehan - in his first Test start at number eight - was held up on the line.

Sheehan was then yellow-carded at the same time as Van Staden, for a croc roll and dangerous clear-out respectively, and while South Africa pushed for a late winner, Ireland held on for a statement win.

Reacting from what looked like a conference room at his team's hotel, Erasmus slammed a table in frustration at full-time before his stream ended, spelling a disappointing end to a tumultuous week for the two-time World Cup-winning coach.

articles.title: Rassie Erasmus: South Africa head coach running the risk of breaching suspension after holding online watchalong
articles.summary: South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus held an online watchalong during the Ireland vs Springboks match in the Nations Championship while serving a suspension from World Rugby; part of Erasmus' ban covers "direct or indirect contact with team management on matchdays"
articles.body:
Erasmus is serving a six-match suspension handed down by World Rugby following extraordinary claims, questioning whether "match-fixing" and "manipulation" was occurring in rugby after his side's defeat to France in Paris last week.

The 54-year-old was suspended for "public criticism of match officials, undermining the integrity of individuals or the sport, and fuelling online abuse".

After a brief welcome, Erasmus kept himself on mute during both halves of the match, where he could be seen clapping at times, gazing intently at a TV, apparently shouting into what presumably was a phone and thumping his table in frustration when Ireland won 20-17.

But he did come off mute at half-time to outline what he thought would be under discussion in the break. He said: "We've not been playing perfect.

"If we step it up I think we'll be in this match. I think they've been really clinical but I'd have been much more worried if we'd played perfect and we're not currently playing perfect and we shouldn't just play to get one bonus point.

"I think will be the gist of what's happening at half-time."

"The suspension applies with immediate effect, applies to international matches, and includes any matchday involvement including coaching, direct or indirect contact with team management or players on matchdays; entering the stadium, coaches' box, playing enclosure, technical area, approaching and/or communicating with match officials on matchday; engaging in any 'feedback' process with match officials; and engaging in media duties during the suspension."

Regarding the "direct or indirect contact with team management or players on matchdays" element of his suspension, Sky Sports sought guidance on the potential for one of South Africa's coaching staff or management set-up signing up, listening to and watching the reactions and comments of their suspended head coach during the contest.

While this specific scenario is not covered by the guidelines, Sky Sports understands Erasmus' plan could be considered a breach by rugby's governing body.

There was, though, a short delay to the broadcast feed Erasmus was using.

South Africa Rugby released a statement requesting a full misconduct hearing in an immediate response to the sanction , but it is understood formal confirmation of an intention to appeal is yet to be received at World Rugby.

Erasmus has now been suspended three times in five years for these sorts of incidents.

During the 2021 British and Irish Lions series in South Africa, after the Springboks lost the first Test, Erasmus broadcast an hour-long critique of Australian referee Nic Berry, and was eventually handed a two-month ban from all rugby activity and a 10-month matchday ban.

In 2022 he received a two-Test ban after sarcastic social media posts following back-to-back South Africa defeats to Ireland and France. A video critical of referee Wayne Barnes led to the official revealing he and his family had received death threats.

On Wednesday, SA Rugby released a statement "condemning the online abuse of officials" following confirmation of Erasmus' ban.

articles.title: Premiership Women's Rugby: Sale Sharks and Trailfinders start season with victories
articles.summary: Gloucester-Hartpury lose their opening PWR match of the season to Sale, two days after the departure of head coach Dan Murphy.
articles.body:
Former champions Gloucester-Hartpury made a losing start to the new Premiership Women's Rugby season, going down 31-17 to Sale Sharks two days after the departure of head coach Dan Murphy.

Murphy's exit was confirmed on Thursday and a replacement head coach is not expected to be in place until January.

Sale's success was their first ever league victory over Gloucester-Hartpury.

After winger Rhona Lloyd had put early points on the board for Sale, Maud Muir and Nel Metcalfe replied to Gloucester-Hartpury move in front.

Although Metcalfe scored again before the end of the first half, further Sale tries from Amy Cokayne (two), Brittany Hogan and Erica Jarrell-Searcy secured victory for the hosts.

The 2026-27 campaign opened with a 29-14 win for Trailfinders over Loughborough Lightning on Friday.

Tries from Meg Jones, Maya Montiel, Hayley Jones, Tanya Kalounivale and Flo Long helped Trailfinders, last season's beaten finalists, begin the season with a bonus-point win.

The opening round of the PWR will conclude on Sunday, with defending champions Saracens hosting Leicester Tigers and Harlequins taking on Bristol Bears.
