articles.title: England 37-12 New Zealand: Can win over All Blacks finally break boom-bust cycle?
articles.summary: Twelve months ago, England beat New Zealand and flopped in the following Six Nations. Can their 2026 success pave the way to more permanent success?
articles.body:
Twelve months ago, as today, England took a famous win over New Zealand.

After a run of victories against lesser opponents, it was the litmus test of their progress. They passed with flying colours and a comfortable scoreline.

It was a statement victory, a sign of things to come. England were building into world-beaters.

The similarities to today's 37-12 success are striking. Even the attendance figure – 81,953 – matches.

For England fans, burned by the dismal Six Nations that followed the 2025 result, there will be a shot of caution with the celebratory drinks tonight.

Steve Borthwick's four-year reign has been marked by booms and busts.

Five defeats in six Tests preceded the 2023 Rugby World Cup, when they came within a point of making the final.

They lost five straight matches in the back half of 2024, before embarking on 12-Test winning streak at the start of 2025.

The sunny uplands have too often turned out to be false dawns.

But, there are grounds to think this time, just maybe, is different.

For a start, it is a different England team, playing a different way.

When the team was named on Thursday, it was striking that England's backline contained none of the same starters as 12 months ago.

Steward, Roebuck, Lawrence, Dingwall, Feyi-Waboso, Ford and Mitchell read the teamsheet for the 2025 win over New Zealand.

Furbank, Murley, Slade, Atkinson, Joseph, Smith, and Van Poortvliet was its 2026 equivalent.

But for injury, Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Alex Mitchell may have featured in both. Tommy Freeman likewise.

The class of 2026, with Fin Smith pulling strings, Henry Slade distributing to pace out wide, and George Furbank out the back and at first receiver, is a more fluid unit.

Seb Atkinson, up against Jordie Barrett, was critical to England's variety, able to combine full-throated midfield carries with deft hands.

Twelve months ago, kicking and chasing was in vogue. And England were setting the trend.

In their 2025 win over the All Blacks, England put boot to ball 35 times and passed it 104 times. A ratio of one to three.

This time around, the stat showed 29 kicks to 176 passes. The boot is being used half as much in relative terms.

The change has been forced to a degree. After a law tweak initially made the aerial route profitable last year, defences have found ways to counter, with retreating catchers and pockets of players posted to pick up scraps.

England had to find new dimensions. And they have.

Jack van Poortvliet and Ollie Chessum's tries were created by clever movement and midfield breaks by Cadan Murley and Will Joseph respectively.

From similar positions 12 months ago, England would have been tempted to take to the skies.

The current way of playing is less predictable, and more sustainable as a long-term tactic to threaten the game's superpowers at the backend of next year's Rugby World Cup.

The balance of power up front has tilted further in England's favour as well.

New Zealand were without talismanic captain Ardie Savea and fellow forwards Luke Jacobsen and Shannon Frizell. But still, England's heavy traffic ram-raided through the heart of the visiting pack a startling number of times.

Ben Earl particularly had a field day. The number eight has been a star performer throughout his team's fluctuating form and stamped his authority on this contest with a whopping 33 carries and 138 metres made.

Ellis Genge, Greg Fisilau and George Martin were abrasive off the bench, cementing England's advantage.

Twelve months ago, New Zealand leapt out into a 12-0 lead with two tries in the first 17 minutes. They never looked like piling on points in a similar quickfire way this time around.

The visitors had only three line breaks compared to nine in 2025.

The dominance was near total. The All Blacks were all out of answers.

And England would have been out of sight sooner with a fewer errors in the first half.

"It was a very good performance and what's exciting is we left some points out there - I think we can be even better," Borthwick told BBC Radio 5 Live afterwards.

"No journey of a team is ever linear. There are always ups and downs that you work through. We continue to strive to improve.

"This is a team that has got enormous growth in it and I'm excited about the journey.

"If players keep the attitude they have to want to get better - and you can see that with the defence, because it was a brilliant defensive performance - when you have that level of commitment, what the players can achieve, I'm excited by the possibilities."

England's fans have certainly bought in.

Lewis Moody's appearance alongside the team for the haka, after presenting them their shirts the previous evening, was an invite to emotionally invest that was impossible to turn down.

The manner in which England's players, in the seconds before kick-off, sought Moody out to embrace him spoke of a bond.

The crowd responded to something special and real.

The All Blacks, famed aura faded, were reduced to minor roles.

Beaten last weekend by Wales, their long season is in severe danger of fizzling out.

If so, it is understandable. They have been set the most brutal of schedules.

In the aftermath of July's Nations Championship they have played nine Tests in less than three months. Four of those were away to South Africa, with the final meeting in the Greatest Rivalry series staged in Baltimore to add a few more air miles to their dizzying itinerary.

Battle-hardened can turn to over-cooked quickly. And with Ruben Love, Quinn Tupaea, Caleb Clarke and Leroy Carter out, their backline is as patched up as their pack.

After a superb start to his All Blacks reign, Dave Rennie would be forgiven for wanted to recuperate and regroup.

As it is, his side will probably be back at Allianz Stadium for a rematch against England in the Nations Championship second-placed play-off next Saturday evening.

Presuming France see off Argentina with a bonus point later on Saturday, they will face South Africa in the Sunday's headline fixture for the inaugural title.

There are big Tests down the road for Borthwick's side. Ireland away in the opening round of the Six Nations in February looms large.

But they are measuring up well, compared to their own high watermarks, as well as the rest of the Test game.

articles.title: Big wins for Saracens, Exeter and Newcastle in Cup
articles.summary: Prem Rugby Cup round-up: Saracens go top with win over Harlequins, while Carwyn Tuipulotu scores a hat-trick for Exeter and Newcastle beat Northampton.
articles.body:
Saracens retained their 100% record in this year's Prem Rugby Cup with an emphatic 43-26 derby win over previously undefeated Harlequins.

On a day of big scores across the competition, Quins took an early lead through James Lang and Lucas Friday before the home side stormed back - with Alfie Barbeary, Sione Va'enuku, Noah Caluori and Nathan Michelow all touching down before the break.

The visitors secured a try bonus point after the break through Bryn Bradley and Nick David, but were unable to prevent further touchdowns from Rotimi Segun and Elliot Daly as Saracens seized control of Pool B.

Harlequins remain in second place, three points adrift of their London rivals, with four games to go in the pool stage.

Hat-trick for Tuipulotu as Chiefs thrash Gloucester

Carwyn Tuipulotu scored a hat-trick as Exeter Chiefs demolished Gloucester 59-12 at Sandy Park.

The Chiefs grabbed nine tries in all, with Will Butt, Paul Brown-Bampoe, Charlie Poynton, Tuipolotu crossing the first half, along with new arrival Dallas McLeod, who scored twice in four minutes.

Gloucester finally got on the board through Krystof Wood's second-half brace, but never looked like overhauling the Chiefs' lead and conceded further tries to Poynton and Tuipolotu.

In a tightly contested Pool A, both Exeter and Gloucester are within a point of second-placed Bath, before the reverse fixtures begin in January.

Tuipulotu aims to extend family's rugby tradition

In the day's other match in Pool B, Newcastle Red Bulls trounced Northampton Saints 49-10 at Kingston Park.

Stung by Thomas Rowe's early effort for the visitors, the home side took control, claiming a try bonus point before the break with scores from Cam Jordan, James Harper and a Christian Wade double.

Additional scores for Werner Kok, Josh Hodge and Jordan put the game beyond doubt, before Archie Benson grabbed a late consolation for the Saints.

Newcastle remain in touching distance of second-placed Harlequins, while Saints linger in fourth and will need to win three of their last four pool matches to have any chance of qualifying for the semi-finals.

articles.title: Nations Championship fixtures: France to play South Africa in final as England face New Zealand rematch plus Ireland vs Australia
articles.summary: World Rugby's 12-team Nations Championship launched in 2026, uniting Six Nations sides, Rugby Championship teams, Fiji, Japan; tournament saw Tests in July, November before Finals Weekend at Twickenham Nov 27-29; France to face South Africa, England vs New Zealand, Ireland vs Australia
articles.body:
The last round of regular fixtures for the tournament saw South Africa suffer defeat to Ireland in Dublin, a week on from losing to France in Paris, but owing to New Zealand losing to England at Twickenham - and failing to pick up any bonus points - the Springboks still finished top of the southern hemisphere table.

France defeated Argentina with a bonus point to confirm their place at the top of the northern hemisphere table ahead of England and Ireland.

The Nations Championship finals take place at Allianz Stadium Twickenham over from November 27-29.

Wherever each northern hemisphere nation finishes in their table decides who they will face next weekend, setting up Tests with the corresponding finishers in the southern hemisphere.

As a result, England will face New Zealand in a rematch on Saturday, while Ireland will play Australia on Friday night.

Fourth-placed Scotland will face Argentina on Sunday, fifth-placed Wales play Japan on Saturday, and sixth-placed Italy will face Fiji on Friday, having just lost to them in Udine.

Nations Championship Finals Weekend at Allianz Stadium Twickenham

England vs New Zealand (4.40pm kick-off)

Final: France vs South Africa (4.40pm kick-off)

The Nations Championship is a joint venture between Six Nations and SANZAAR that pits the giants of northern and southern hemisphere rugby against each other on a more consistent basis.

The tournament is designed to align northern and southern hemisphere rugby calendars, guaranteeing high-profile fixtures to add more structure and meaning to the existing international windows between World Cups.

Each team will play six matches: three in July in the southern hemisphere and three in November in the northern hemisphere.

Twickenham's Allianz Stadium will then host Finals Weekend from November 27 to 29, where the inaugural champions will be crowned.

Rankings for Finals Weekend will be determined by results from the opening six matches, with each northern hemisphere team playing an additional fixture against the correspondingly ranked southern side.

Nations Championship - November fixtures and results

Friday November 6 Ireland 42-12 Argentina

Sunday November 8 England 45-22 Australia

Friday November 13 France 21-19 South Africa

Sunday November 15 Scotland 15-12 Australia

articles.title: Nations Championship: Ireland remind themselves that the best are beatable with 20-17 win over South Africa
articles.summary: Ireland put a string of deflating losses against the world's best teams behind them with a hard-fought 20-17 win over South Africa in Dublin.
articles.body:
After six deflating losses in a row to South Africa, New Zealand and France, Andy Farrell was asked this week what made him think Ireland could get back to the levels they had reached when considered squarely among that group.

Because they had got there before came the typically uncomplicated response from the side's head coach.

The longer the 2023 World Cup receded into memory, however, fewer and fewer believed that his side still had within them the type of performance they produced to beat the Springboks 20-17 on Saturday.

Undoubtedly Ireland's biggest win of recent years, having not beaten one of the three sides who started this weekend above them in the rankings since the summer of 2024, this was one of their most needed too.

This Test had long been viewed as one of the crucial measuring sticks for Farrell's side building towards next autumn's World Cup - the last time they will face the back-to-back champions before boarding the plane to Australia.

Having settled into a pattern where they could not beat the best, but almost always found a way past the rest, Ireland could not have headed down under with genuine belief of making history without first showing they were still capable of this level.

"It's something that we've been looking forward to, to challenge ourselves and delivering when it matters against top-line sides," said Farrell.

"We knew that this fixture was coming, playing against the world's best by a stretch at this moment in time

"It was a game that we we wanted to challenge ourselves and see how we went and, obviously fronting up and showing the character that we did, and coming out on the right side of the win is a big night for everyone who is Irish."

Farrell defends Prendergast after SA camp comments

For all that had gone on in the build-up, from explosive news conferences to coaching suspensions, from dismissed citing complaints to eye-catching positional switches , by the time of kick-off, it almost felt as if a reminder was needed that there was still a game to be played.

Some two hours later, with the banned Rassie Erasmsus having watched on from a nearby hotel with only a host of virtual followers on a near-silent YouTube stream for company, his Springboks side had lost consecutive games for the first time in four years.

If his comments this week were designed to illicit a response from his side after last week's loss to France, he did not get the desired reaction. Instead, it was Ireland who it seemed had appropriately fuelled the fire.

Virtually scrummaged off the park in this fixture last year, prop Andrew Porter was among those who said that day had stuck with them in the months since.

While the tables were not turned at scrum-time, rather than allow the set-piece to again become the dominant thread of the game, this time around Ireland weathered the storm and came out the other side.

Their aerial work in particular was key, with Farrell typically highlighting Robert Baloucoune's efforts to regather possession before mentioning the winger's second double in as many weeks.

"We were very good at just getting on with it," added the head coach.

"It's not always going to go your way against the world's best, certainly at scrum-time, they're world-leading in that regard. We took everything in isolation and just kept going on to the next moment.

"That was the story of the game, really."

Even if South Africa had wrestled the game back in those frantic closing moments, this would not have been a loss to catalogue alongside the others against South Africa, France and New Zealand in recent years.

Having started 2026 with their intent questioned after defeat in Paris, Ireland played their last home game of the year showing an appreciation that in these sorts of contests, it is the small moments that make for big results.

A first-half scrum penalty of their own was greeted as raucously as a score while, whether it be a Joe McCarthy maul turnover, Mack Hansen's try-saving tackle on Canan Moodie or Hugo Keenan eating up the ground to thwart Kurt-Lee Arendse, Ireland continued to show that this time they were to stay in the fight.

There will still be talk of whether this was truly Ireland absorbing South Africa's best punch - with both the Boks and All Blacks having lost twice in succession, questions will be asked of how much the four-Test Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series has taken out of both sides.

"We're not playing to our best potential," said captain Siya Kolisi.

"We know as a group we have better. I don't question the effort or the mindset, but it's executing better."

Still, Ireland must believe that this was a game that said more about themselves than their opponents.

articles.title: France 45-17 Argentina - Les Bleus secure final spot
articles.summary: France dispatch Argentina in Paris to book their spot against South Africa in the Nations Championship final at Allianz Stadium next Sunday.
articles.body:
Tries: Guillard, Mauvaka, Gourgues 2, Gailleton, Duguid, Bielle-Biarrey Cons: Gourgues 5

Tries: Piccardo, Matera Cons: Albornoz 2 Pen: Albornoz

France dispatched Argentina in Paris to book their spot against South Africa in the Nations Championship final at Allianz Stadium next Sunday.

Knowing pre-game a bonus-point victory at Stade de France would be enough to edge England out of the top spot in the northern hemisphere standings, Les Bleus had to work hard to secure the points required.

Lock Mickael Guillard powered over for the opening score, but Justo Piccardo responded for the visitors before Tomas Albornoz nudged them ahead with a penalty.

Argentina have not been at their best this November, suffering a heavy defeat by Ireland before narrowly beating Italy.

However, as is often the case with the Pumas, the longer they spend together, the more they tend to improve as a campaign progresses.

Felipe Contepomi's side brought the first-half physicality needed to trouble France, who turned to their maul late in the first half to score through Peato Mauvaka and reclaim the lead.

Fly-half Matthieu Jalibert, who missed the win over the world champions through injury, then expertly sent Kalvin Gourgues through a gap to score.

The pivotal moment came when Argentina prop Mayco Vivas was shown a 20-minute red card for making direct head contact at a ruck, with France capitalising on the extra man to score their bonus-point try through Emilien Gailleton.

Hooker Julian Montoya then joined Vivas in the sin-bin after receiving a yellow card and France made their numerical advantage count once again as Tyler Duguid and Gourgues crossed.

Pablo Matera intercepted Louis Bielle-Biarrey's pass to improve the scoreline but Bielle-Biarrey made amends to dot down a brilliant kick into space by Antoine Dupont.

It will now be rematch of last Friday's epic game in Paris, which France narrowly won 21-19 against the world champions.

South Africa booked their spot in the final by picking up a losing bonus point against Ireland.

Scotland will play Argentina on Sunday at Allianz Stadium in the seventh/eighth-place play-off.

articles.title: Wales 26-29 Australia: Wallabies hold on for Nations Championship win in Cardiff
articles.summary: Wales could not emulate their famous victory against New Zealand as Australia claimed the Nations Championship spoils in Cardiff.
articles.body:
Tries: Lake 2, Murray, Elias Cons: Costelow 3

Tries: Tupou, Paenga-Amosa, Jorgensen, Ikitau Cons: Lonergan 2, Gordon Pens: Gordon

Wales could not emulate their famous victory against New Zealand as Australia claimed the Nations Championship spoils in Cardiff.

The Wallabies ended a four-match losing run thanks to tries from hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa, prop Taniela Tupou, wing Max Jorgensen and centre Len Ikitau, while fly-half Carter Gordon kicked a late penalty.

Wales captain Dewi Lake scored two tries, while full-back Blair Murray also crossed following a superb assist by wing Louis Rees-Zammit.

Replacement hooker Ryan Elias grabbed a late try but Australia held on for victory as Wales paid the price for not capitalising on attacking chances.

Wales finished fifth in the northern hemisphere section and will play Japan at the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham on Saturday (13:10 GMT).

Australia finished third in the southern hemisphere table and play Ireland on Friday (20:10 GMT).

Fans flock back to the Principality Stadium

After all the hysteria and celebrations to mark a first victory against the All Blacks in 73 years, the attention turned towards whether Wales could back it up against Australia.

There was a vibrancy on the streets of Cardiff before the game not seen for a while, which reflected in the crowd.

After crowds of 52,425 against Japan and 55,152 against New Zealand, the 66,307 attendance against Australia was the highest of the autumn.

The All Blacks win proved instrumental in a surge of tickets sold for a 20:10 GMT kick-off, the latest for a Wales rugby home game at the Principality Stadium.

Head coach Steve Tandy made four changes to revert to the side that beat Japan with flanker James Botham the most notable absentee following his player-of-the-match against New Zealand.

Botham was expecting the birth of his first child this week but Tandy stated his omission was for rugby reasons with Cardiff colleague Alex Mann replacing him.

Fit-again number eight Aaron Wainwright replaced Taine Basham, while lock Ben Carter and wing Josh Adams returned for Adam Beard and Gabriel Hamer-Webb.

Australia had freshened things up with five forward changes as flanker Carlo Tizzano, lock Tom Hooper and the front-row trio of Isaac Kailea, Paenga-Amosa and Tupou came in.

Australia open scoring after Llewellyn yellow card

Wales lost centre Max Llewellyn inside two minutes to a yellow card for a high tackle on Wallabies full-back Tom Wright.

Wallabies had plenty of early possession against 14 players but the home defence comfortably dealt with the attack.

Mann was caught with some friendly fire by a finger in the eye from team-mate Carter but continued despite appearing to have vision issues.

Rees-Zammit almost squeezed into the corner but just failed to ground the ball under pressure from Gordon, before Lake was held up over the Australia line.

Mann, despite his eye seeming to be closing, was still able to force a turnover penalty but Wales were guilty of early handling errors.

After Wales won a scrum penalty, the officials then either missed Tupou striking Mann with a body jab, or deemed it did not warrant further action.

Tupou stayed on the field to open the scoring in the 21st minute as he evaded Llewellyn's tackle to cross for an unconverted try.

Wales retaliated quickly with Morgan breaking away and feeding scrum-half Tomos Williams, who was held up by superb visiting defence.

There were important turnover penalties from Tizzano and Tupou who benefitted from a huge tackle from Australia captain Harry Wilson on opposite number Wainwright.

The hosts held the upper hand in the first-half aerial battle but Wales were not as clinical as they were against New Zealand.

Australia centre Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii gained an intercept before being hauled down by Rees-Zammit, who conceded a penalty.

Wallabies demonstrated a more ruthless approach as Paenga-Amosa was driven over.

Mann continued to wind up the Australia forwards, which helped gain 10 metres for dissent, but Wales continued to waste chances as an attacking line-out was stolen.

Morgan was a Wales carrying colossus in the first half with a series of impressive bursts and the home side finally gained a reward in the 40th minute when Lake dived over with Costelow converting.

Australia led 12-7 at half-time with Wales having an on-pitch huddle before heading to their changing room.

Wallabies aerial dominance proves crucial

Suaalii towered over Murray to take an early second-half attacking high ball but Wallabies were denied a try by a brilliant Morgan turnover.

Australia scrum-half Lonergan missed a penalty before Wallabies' second-half aerial dominance was rewarded when Jorgensen rose above Adams before finishing off the move to score.

Wales brought on a raft of replacements, including an early introduction for scrum-half Reuben Morgan-Williams.

The changes worked when Lake was driven over for his second score before Wales followed up with a magical try.

Rees-Zammit was the architect with a stunning outside break before feeding Adams who provided the try-scoring pass to Murray.

Costelow's conversion gave Wales the lead for the first time.

Australia hold on for first win in five matches

Australia brought on experienced forward replacements with Fraser McReight and Angus Bell making immediate impacts.

Prop Allan Alaalatoa appeared to have scored on his 99th international, but it was ruled out following a knock-on by replacement scrum-half Kalani Thomas.

The Wallabies wave continued with Wales duo Eddie James and Archie Griffin producing impressive tackles before Ikitau restored the visitors' lead.

Morgan left the field for a head injury assessment (HIA) to be replaced by Kane James, who was in tears when the anthem was played as he marked his first Wales appearance in Cardiff.

Fellow replacement Louie Hennessey knocked on to give Australia an attacking platform before Wainwright conceded a penalty which Carter kicked to take the Wallabies two scores clear.

Morgan returned and Wales responded as they battered the Australia line with Wilson shown a yellow card.

Elias was driven over to secure two losing bonus-points and set up a grandstand finale, but Wallabies held on for a vital victory for head coach Les Kiss.

Replacements: Elias, G Thomas, Lewis, Plumtree, K James, Morgan-Williams, Hawkins, Hennessey.

Assistant referees: Karl Dickson (England) & Jeremy Rozier (France).

articles.title: Nations Championship: Wales fall short in 29-26 defeat to Australia after epic New Zealand victory
articles.summary: Australia narrowly defeated Wales at the Principality stadium in Cardiff; Wales couldn't follow up the previous week's epic victory over New Zealand, their first over the All Blacks since 1953; Wales to face Japan on Finals Weekend with Australia taking on Ireland
articles.body:
A first victory over the All Blacks since 1953 had led to week-long celebrations in Wales.

But Australia, having soaked up fierce first-half pressure, produced some fine attacking rugby after the break to prevent Wales from winning three on the spin for the first time since the 2023 World Cup.

Taniela Tupou, Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Max Jorgensen and Len Ikitau secured a try-bonus point for Australia as Ryan Lonergan and Carter Gordon added nine points with the boot.

Wales also scored four tries through Dewi Lake's double, Blair Murray and Ryan Elias, with Sam Costelow landing three conversions, but fell agonisingly short.

Australia fly-half Carter Gordon scored ⁠a penalty in the 74th minute to give the Wallabies a 29-21 lead, which proved enough for victory despite Wales securing a fourth try ⁠through replacement hooker Elias two minutes ​from time.

Wales battled for the winning score in a dramatic close to the match but their attempt to go the length of the field was ended when the ball was ‌knocked on.

"Wales are a tough outfit. What a match," Ikitau said after he was awarded player of the match.

"It's been a tough couple of weeks for us. I know the heart's always there but when you don't get the results it's pretty disheartening. I'm proud of the boys and proud of the effort today."

articles.title: France book South Africa rematch in Nations Championship final with bonus-point victory over Argentina
articles.summary: France beat Argentina 45-17, securing the bonus-point victory they needed to reach the final of the Nations Championship; France will meet South Africa in the November 29 final at Twickenham; France beat the Springboks 21-19 last week in Paris
articles.body:
England's 37-12 win against New Zealand left France needing a bonus-point victory to make the November 29 final against South Africa, who topped the southern hemisphere group despite losing to Ireland.

Already leading 21-10, Emilien Gailleton got France's fourth try for the bonus point in the 64th minute against 14 men, and moments later the yellow card for Pumas prop Mayco Vivas was upgraded to red.

France finished with three more tries. Lock Tyler Duguid charged through following an attacking lineout, centre Kalvin Gourgues showed stunning pace from near halfway to make the left corner, and Louis Bielle-Biarrey completed the rout with his 31st try in 30 tests.

In the first half lock Mickaël Guillard and try-scoring hooker Peato Mauvaka crossed for France. Returning fly-half Matthieu Jalibert cleverly set up silky centre Gourgues shortly after the break for the first of his two tries.

Argentina led briefly at 10-7 for 10 minutes thanks to a converted try from centre Justo Piccardo and a penalty from fly-half Tomas Albornoz.

Jalibert's faster than expected recovery from a torn thigh allowed captain Antoine Dupont to resume at scrum-half after wearing the No 10 jersey a week ago against South Africa.

Dupont showed his class at the end with a kick down the left flank for Bielle-Biarrey's try.

Gourdes nailed five conversions as a makeshift kicker on the night.

Tributes were held before the game for Federico Martín Aramburú, the former Argentina player who died four years ago after being fatally shot in Paris.

articles.title: Wales 26-29 Australia: Steve Tandy frustrated by Nations Championship defeat
articles.summary: Wales head coach Steve Tandy said he was frustrated after his side failed to back up their epic win over New Zealand with victory against Australia.
articles.body:
Wales head coach Steve Tandy said he was frustrated as his side failed to back up their epic win over New Zealand, narrowly losing to Australia.

The Wallabies edged the Nations Championship Test 29-26 in Cardiff on Saturday, a week after a first Wales victory over the All Blacks since 1953 had led to wild celebrations.

Taniela Tupou, Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Max Jorgensen and Len Ikitau secured a try-bonus point for Australia as Ryan Lonergan and Carter Gordon added nine points with the boot.

Wales also scored four tries, through Dewi Lake's double, Blair Murray and Ryan Elias, with Sam Costelow landing three conversions.

"The overarching feeling is the frustration of losing," said Tandy.

"We were disappointed. We probably weren't as accurate as we could have been. We were held up three times and could have gone ahead on the scoreboard."

The 46-year-old former Ospreys coach added: "Maybe we needed a little bit of composure but there were enough opportunities to come away with the win.

"I know it's not the result anyone wanted but the supporters were amazing again."

Despite the loss, and that frustration, the Wales head coach praised his side's attitude in attempting to follow up their historic win against the All Blacks.

"Fair play to the boys, after such a monumental game last week with the emotional energy, we stuck in the game and scored four tries," he said.

"So there are a lot of positives in the performance to take as well."

Australia hold on for narrow win against Wales

Nations Championship - Australia triumph over Wales - reaction

Australia, having soaked up fierce first-half pressure, produced some fine attacking rugby after the break to prevent Wales from winning three matches in a row for the first time since the 2023 World Cup.

"It's sport, you have major highs and then lows, and that's the game we play," said skipper Lake.

"Our frustration comes from the fact that we probably weren't at our best.

"We created opportunities during large parts of the game, but there were little inaccuracies at the wrong times."

Lake, however, said he could not fault the effort of the squad.

"We spoke about backing up last weekend, and we didn't back it up with a result but I think we backed it up with effort and energy," said the captain.

"We had opportunities to win that game, but unfortunately it wasn't to be for us today.

"We'll fix those accuracy issues and we'll be ready to go again next week."

Wales will face Japan at the Allianz Stadium at Twickenham on Saturday (13:10 GMT) after both sides finished fifth in the two Nations Championship tables - north and south.

It will be a fifth time Wales and Japan have met in 16 months with Tandy's side defeating Eddie Jones' team 28-21 in Cardiff just two weeks ago.

Wales have an injury doubt over scrum-half Tomos Williams who has a tight groin, with Tandy expected to make a number changes to freshen up the side.

Australia grateful for breaking losing sequence

Australia head coach Les Kiss was happy to have broken a four-match losing sequence which included recent defeats against Scotland and England.

"I am not only proud but also happy for these boys," said Kiss.

"The work they've been putting in over the last four weeks has been good and they just haven't been getting a reward.

"Hats off to Wales. They beat the All Blacks here last week but didn't seem to lack any verve or energy.

"That didn't take it out of them and actually created more energy and confidence in them."

Captain Harry Wilson said it was a special to end the Wallabies' poor sequence.

"When you have four losses on the bounce, you question a few things," said the back-row forward.

"Rugby is such a results-driven game and we hadn't been getting the results even though I felt like we weren't far off last week.

"To beat a team who just had defeated the All Blacks, in front of 65,000 Wales supporters where the atmosphere was crazy, was special."

The Wallabies will now face Ireland on Friday in the contest for fifth place in Twickenham (20:10 GMT) after both sides finished third in their respective pools.

articles.title: Jonathan Davies compares WRU to Man Utd but backs new chairman Lyndon Faulkner
articles.summary: Former Wales captain Jonathan Davies says new Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) chairman Lyndon Faulkner can turn Welsh rugby around.
articles.body:
Former Wales captain Jonathan Davies says new Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) chairman Lyndon Faulkner is the man to turn Welsh rugby around.

The former Newport and Pontypool forward, who takes over from Richard Collier-Keywood , attends his first WRU annual general meeting (AGM) on Sunday.

He has already promised to review everything including the controversial plan to cut a men's professional side by 2028.

Faulkner has forged a highly successful business career in the United States of America.

The 66-year-old also has a Welsh rugby background as the nephew of former Wales prop Charlie Faulkner, who was inducted into World Rugby's hall of fame on Saturday alongside Bobby Windsor and Graham Price - the famed Pontypool front row.

Former Wales fly-half Davies, who called for the WRU board to resign before Faulkner's appointment, believes the new chair will galvanise Welsh rugby off the field.

“I believe the chair is a good guy and he has the opportunity to change things and he will make them,” said Davies.

“He is a successful businessman, but he is a rugby man."

Davies has described the problems at the WRU as similar to football giants Manchester United.

“When I look at Manchester United, I also look at the WRU," Davies told BBC Radio 5 Live Sport.

"When United changed and brought the bankers in there was no football knowledge and the same has happened in Welsh rugby."

The former Wales captain said decisions that have been made by the union have been purely financial, and not rugby ones.

“Lyndon is the right man and will make the necessary changes in the WRU to give these guys a better platform," Davies added.

“It’s not going to happen overnight and if we don‘t make these changes we will be in tier two for a long time.”

Davies believes the WRU needs to help the players who earlier this month inspired the nation with a first victory against New Zealand in 73 years, a match played in front of just over 55,000 fans.

“I heard [captain] Dewi Lake say something before the New Zealand game and I felt really sorry for the players," said Davies.

“He said because the attendance was low that was down to them. I felt sad the players felt like that.

“[Welsh rugby] is a real sideshow at the moment with the players taking the brunt of it and Dewi and Jac [Morgan] have gone to Gloucester where, from what I have heard, they have changed the culture and are two great guys.

“Nobody blames the players for where they are, it’s the WRU’s job.

“The New Zealand win shows what the players are capable of, given the right platform.”

Faulkner has also indicated he is a fan of an Anglo-Welsh competition, something with witch Davies agrees.

Prem Rugby in England has opened a registration process for teams to apply with the aim of expanding the league to 12 clubs for the 2029-30 season.

Plans to grow the league from the current 10 clubs were confirmed in February, with a 'request for information' stage now open until 1 February 2027.

Clubs, investors and their authorised representatives have been invited to register their interest in joining the English top tier, although a statement said that no formal bid or commitment to invest is required to do so.

The Prem and the Rugby Football Union (RFU) have previously insisted they will consider an English expansion but their press release this week made no mention of only English clubs applying, with Welsh interest in the proposal.

“I think Wales would add to the Prem,” said Davies.

“It’s a brilliant competition already and having Welsh sides in there would benefit Welsh rugby enormously.”

Time for WRU to match team's leadership - Davies

Prem reluctant to commit on Anglo-Welsh league

The Prem has consisted of 10 clubs since the 2022-23 season, when Wasps, Worcester and London Irish all folded within the space of a few months.

Promotion and relegation to and from the league was also scrapped as of this season.

Previous conditions said teams would need to compete in the second-tier Champ for a season before being eligible to play in the Prem, and that any bids would be assessed on a range of criteria including finances, investment potential, infrastructure and how their geographical base could help spread the Prem's appeal.

Earlier this month RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney confirmed the WRU had asked to join the Prem and form an Anglo-Welsh league.

Wales currently has four professional sides - Scarlets, Ospreys, Cardiff and Dragons - who play in the United Rugby Championship (URC), although the WRU plans to cut one of the teams by 2028 because of financial issues.

A statement from Prem Rugby and the RFU in October said that the focus was on expanding the league with English clubs although Sweeney confirmed just over a week later that they had been approached by the WRU and that discussions would continue.

The URC has so far not commented on one of its shareholders courting another competition.

The WRU has also not publicly responded to Sweeney's comments about its approach to the RFU but will face questions about the issue at the AGM.

articles.title: Scotland: Let promising Liam McConnell loose against Argentina
articles.summary: Scotland head into their Nations Championship finale against Argentina on a high and should unleash Liam McConnell on the Pumas after his hat-trick against Japan, writes Tom English.
articles.body:
Having lost at home to Argentina in November and then beating Argentina away from home in July, Scotland's next joust with the Pumas is set for Twickenham next Sunday, 29 November - fourth from the northern hemisphere versus fourth from the south on the final day of the Nations Championship.

The warm-up act before the grand final between France and South Africa later on Sunday is not where Scotland wanted to be, but four wins from six games is a decent return.

A fifth win in seven would be encouraging, if not life-changing for this team. They've all been at this rodeo before.

On Saturday, Scotland's much-changed team tore an understrength, over-powered and severely out-matched Japan to shreds. Eleven tries was bordering on an exhibition.

It didn't tell us anything we didn't already know about head coach Gregor Townsend's set-up, but it was a special day for a number of people, chief among them the fantastically promising Liam McConnell and the revitalised Darcy Graham - hat-tricks for both and a ton of other wonderful moments besides.

Hat-trick hero Graham pushing to reclaim starting berth

Scotland kept 'foot on throat' in ruthless display - captain McDowall

McConnell shines as 11-try Scotland dismantle Japan

That Scotland had far too much speed, skill, power and ruthlessness for Japan was not surprising. They scored some blistering tries.

These are fine rugby players, albeit ones who are, just like the players they took over from, prone to giving up soft moments; avoidable penalties, easy entries into their own 22, self-inflicted stress on their own defence, which was strong on Saturday.

Scotland gave up seven penalties in the first half against Japan. The visitors weren't good enough to break their hosts down from all that field position, but the teams that Scotland want to start beating certainly would have been.

New Zealand were more than good enough only a few weeks ago. It was a large part of Scotland's fall that day.

In public, Townsend accentuates the positives, as he must - and there was plenty of positivity to go around. His team delivered a thunderous and classy win.

Privately, he has to be looking at the indiscipline of the first half - it was near- perfect in the second - and cursing it.

Japan were never going to punish them, but in defining games in the Six Nations against heavy hitters, and in the knockouts of the World Cup against bigger beasts, then he knows what's going to happen if that stuff gets repeated.

This is unforgiving terrain. Scotland are desperate to move closer to a higher level and so they will be brutal on each other - or should be.

We saw what that level was all about on Saturday - a fast-improving England brutalising the All Blacks, who have now lost back-to-back, and a ferociously physical Ireland taking down the Springboks, who have also now lost two-in-a-row.

The standard is savagely high. Critics of Townsend say that Scotland haven't improved on his watch because they haven't won any trophies. That pays no regard to the improvement that other nations have made in the Townsend years.

It's not like the biggest countries are standing still. South Africa aren't, France aren't.

Ireland looked for a while like they were falling away a touch but now they appear to be back. England are flying.

New Zealand are a work-in-progress, but they were too much for Scotland. Scotland are moving forward, but for all the tries and all the thrills they can produce, they have a long way to go, if they get there at all. They know that better than anybody.

Murrayfield was heaving again on Saturday, a capacity crowd for the visit of Japan, 12,000 more fans for this game against the world number 12 than turned up at the Principality Stadium last weekend for Wales playing the All Blacks.

We should pause for a second there because the strength of the Scotland support in difficult times is quite something. It's easy to sell-out the marquee games, but doing it against Japan on Saturday and against Fiji last season is impressive.

It follows on from more than 56,000 against the USA and more than 60,000 against Tonga last autumn and another 60,000-plus against Portugal in the autumn of 2024.

More than 55,000 were at the Georgia game in the summer of 2023. Huge numbers for a nation that hasn't won a tournament - or even come close to winning a tournament - in 27 years.

They go again at Twickenham. Another weekend and another Test and a challenging one at that.

Scotland are losing players at an alarming rate; Matt Fagerson and Nathan McBeth got injured against Japan and almost certainly won't make for the fourth-placed play-off.

For the Japan game, Townsend was without the injured Pierre Schoeman, Elliot Millar Mills, Scott Cummings, Alex Craig, Jamie Ritchie, Jack Dempsey, Rory Darge, Sione Tuipulotu, Fergus Burke and Ben White.

Scotland's depth in most of those positions is sound, but with Schoeman out and McBeth probably on his way out, things are looking fragile. Rory Sutherland and Alec Hepburn look set for the looseheads spots at Twickenham.

One of the big, and happy, conundrums facing Townsend and his coaches in the coming days is what to do with the tearaway McConnell. Unleash against the Pumas from the start? Put him on the bench for impact? Or cut him from the 23, a move that wouldn't go down well.

He has verve and pace and a work ethic that makes him a huge prospect. This game at Twickenham is an odd thing - one that Scotland will really want to win for feelgood sake but also the last opportunity for a while to give the McConnells another chance to show their stuff.

Once Scotland hit the Six Nations, it'll be full metal jacket stuff. Their World Cup warm-ups are all serious business - home and away against France and away to the All Blacks.

There's a little space to experiment there, but not much. Townsend shouldn't be in a rush to change things for Twickenham. McConnell warrants another start.

He's exciting and intriguing. Let the boy fly.

articles.title: Ireland 20-17 South Africa: Did hosts 'change the narrative' against the Springboks?
articles.summary: After a 20-17 win on Saturday, did Ireland's victory over South Africa change the narrative for Andy Farrell's side?
articles.body:
Ten months out from the World Cup, Ireland needed to make a statement.

They had lost their last six matches against South Africa, New Zealand and France, and questions were starting to be asked if this was an Irish team past their best.

A year ago, South Africa had demolished the Irish scrum on their way to a 24-13 win in Dublin.

But on Saturday, it was Ireland who came out on top with a 20-17 victory as Andy Farrell's side blocked out the pre-match noise after Rassie Erasmus' six-game ban.

"We knew what a lot of the players were capable of, but for them to come out and do that just changes the narrative around the Irish rugby team," former Ireland scrum-half Conor Murray said on the Ireland Rugby Social podcast.

"To do that to the world champions, and there were some whispers from the South Africans that they weren't great, but we made them look average with the physicality and the scrum.

"Everyone looked so up for it. It changes the feeling of it."

Ireland remind themselves that the best are beatable

Farrell defends Prendergast after SA camp comments

Former Ireland forward Mike McCarthy said it was a "phenomenal performance" as Robert Baloucoune scored two tries and Ronan Kelleher also crossed in Dublin.

Despite having a mixed game with the boot, Sam Prendergast ultimately kicked the decisive points as Ireland held off a late fightback from the back-to-back world champions.

"Everyone wrote them off pre-game. The boys have had to live with that for a year, when they capitulated at scrum time," he said.

"All the talk was how South Africa were hurting after the France game and they would do it for Rassie, but it was phenomenal from every player."

Speaking to the podcast after the game, Ireland back row Josh van der Flier said it was "one of those special days".

"It's brilliant and the lads dug deep. South Africa are a brilliant side and everyone knows how good they are.

"We worked unbelievably hard, and we're delighted to get the result."

In contrast to the roar of 70,000 supporters in the Aviva, egged on by Ryan Baird at every scrum, Erasmus sat alone in South Africa's team hotel in Dublin.

It came after South Africa's head coach was handed a six-game ban over comments he made about match officials in his side's Nations Championship defeat by France

Instead of shying away from it, Erasmus hosted a watchalong on YouTube. Bar one set of comments at half-time, it turned out to be in near silence as he sat in an empty conference room.

A one point, a member of staff was clearing chairs away in the background.

But the slamming of the desk as South Africa lost the ball in the final play said more than any words could, before Erasmus hastily packed his laptop away.

After a defeat by France the previous week, losing in Dublin was the first time the Springboks had lost back-to-back matches in four years.

South Africa still topped the southern hemisphere table, but it has proven the best in the world are still beatable.

"We actually didn't talk about it. If anything it was a bit of motivation," said van der Flier on the pre-game noise, in which Prendergast was also cleared of a citing from the previous win over Fiji.

"We talked about playing rugby well and not getting into any of the chat. I've anything rugby-related muted on my phone so I could ignore it all.

"It happens every week, but especially against South Africa where there's more chat than normal."

Despite finishing on 24 points - which would have been enough to finish top of the southern hemisphere table - Ireland had to settle for third behind France and England.

The victory made it three wins from three in November, after big victories over Argentina and Fiji at the start of the month.

That means they will face Australia on Friday in a fifth-place play-off, and McCarthy feels it is a "shame" to follow up the Springboks' game with what he feels is a "dead rubber".

However, Murray pointed to the World Cup next year, and believes it could be a chance to follow up a big win with another strong performance - something that could happen in knock out rugby in Australia.

"This was such a high, but if you fast forward to a World Cup and you end up playing a big team in a quarter-final, you still have to show up the next week.

"Andy will frame it like that. This could happen down the line, to see if you can go and repeat it.

"That's what tournaments and World Cups are like. This was the peak, but now you have to go and do it again."

For van der Flier, the playing group will not look beyond next week.

"We have probably disappointed ourselves in the past year with a good performance and then a bad one, but it's been good in this period with three wins," he said.

"Hopefully we can keep building that momentum into next week and into next year."

articles.title: Ellis Genge calls on England to follow New Zealand victory with another win over All Blacks in Nations Championship
articles.summary: England thrashed New Zealand 37-12 at the Allianz Stadium on Saturday and will face each other again on Saturday, having both finished second in their respective Nations Championship groups; England also beat New Zealand last November
articles.body:
The rivals face an immediate rematch of England's 37-12 procession at Allianz Stadium that meant they each finished second in their Nations Championship pools, setting up the battle for third place on Saturday.

Following on from last November's 33-19 triumph , it was only the second time in the fixture's 121-year existence that England had registered consecutive wins - and Steve Borthwick's men are aiming to carve out their own piece of history.

"Try and emulate it, do the same thing again," Genge said. "It's as simple as it sounds. I don't think you can take anything away from New Zealand. They're not any less of a beast next weekend than what the challenge was this week.

"New Zealand tends to be one team that catches you off guard, but what shocks you is that they're actually quite direct.

"You think they're all traditionally very good at moving the ball, but they're very punchy and we got that right against them."

England delivered the best result of Borthwick's four years in charge by flattening the All Blacks to extend their winning run to five Tests and issue a warning that they will be genuine contenders at next year's World Cup.

But amid the euphoria that has greeted confirmation of their post-Six Nations revival, Genge will keep perspective - recalling the criticism their followed their 45-21 drubbing at Ellis Park in the Nations Championship opener .

"Sport's fickle in that sense," Genge said. "We were the worst team in the world against South Africa when we got hammered at their gaff about five months ago.

"Then we hammered Fiji because of a red card apparently, then scraped past Argentina and then now we're the best thing since sliced bread. It's one of them.

"Sometimes the outside noise can creep in. Sometimes it can build you up and that's a long way down to the bottom.

"You've got to try and just keep your head on your shoulders and just build results. We do as best as we can at the job to keep everyone's head on their shoulders, especially with a young squad.

"Some of us miserable old boys are a bit easier, but the boys get so excited to play and be a part of it, which is brilliant. You've got to prepare them for that as well."

Seb Atkinson was the last of England's five tryscorers at Allianz Stadium and he marked the crowning moment of a stellar individual performance by sticking out his tongue and making a throat-slitting gesture.

The celebration has been mistaken online as a reference to the All Blacks' haka, but Atkinson revealed it was born out of his interest in gladiatorial combat and is deciding whether to make it his calling card.

"I've had a bit of stick already on that, so we'll see whether it stays," Atkinson said. "It's a gladiator celebration. I used to have a big interest in Roman history so it was bit of a gladiatorial theme from when they used to do it in the Colosseum.

"I enjoyed learning about that when I was growing up and I trialled it with Gloucester and then I felt like I had to give it a bit extra today [Saturday]."

Atkinson is expected to feature again for England against New Zealand next week and hopes the hosts can take a leaf out of South Africa's book by showing the hunger to evolve like the back-to-back world champions.

"Any professional team, any sporting team, always wants to strive to get better because a team that gets caught still is in trouble," he added. "That's what the South Africans have done really well over the last period.

"Their game has been transformed. We'll be focusing on ourselves, but with an eye just to keep getting better and see what we can do."
